# ACT New Zealand

> Party founded in 1994; Wikipedia's infobox describes it as classical-liberal and right-libertarian, and places it on the right. It has been a junior partner in the National-led coalition since November 2023.
> **Leader:** [David Seymour](./people/david-seymour/README.md) (since October 2014). He has been Deputy Prime Minister since 31 May 2025 and is also Minister for Regulation.
> **Deputy leader:** [Nicole McKee](./people/nicole-mckee/README.md) (since 28 June 2026, replacing Brooke van Velden, who is retiring at the election). **President:** John Windsor.

- 2026 policies: **[./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md)**
- Track record (promises vs delivery, reliability, alignment): **[./track-record.md](./track-record.md)**
- Promise data: [`data/promises/act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json)

## Quick facts

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 1993 as the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers (pressure group); party from 1994. Founders: Sir Roger Douglas and Derek Quigley |
| Ideology | Classical liberalism, right-libertarianism, conservatism (Wikipedia); describes itself as standing for "one law for all", smaller government and individual freedom |
| Seats (54th Parliament) | 11 of 123: Epsom (Seymour), Tāmaki (van Velden) and 9 list MPs |
| 2023 party vote | 8.64% (246,409 votes), its best result ever |
| 2026 polling | Roughly 6–11% across 2026 polls. In October 2026 polls: 9–11% |
| In government | Support partner for National 2008–2017. Coalition partner since 2023: 3 Cabinet ministers plus ministers outside Cabinet |

## History

**Origins (1993–2004).** ACT grew out of the "Backbone Club" of Labour MPs who backed Roger Douglas's free-market reforms ("Rogernomics"). It began as a pressure group and became a party to contest the first MMP election. Its platform was based on Douglas's book *Unfinished Business*. Under Richard Prebble (leader 1996–2004) it won 6.1% in 1996, 7.0% in 1999 and 7.1% in 2002.

**Collapse and the Epsom lifeline (2005–2011).** After Prebble left, ACT fell to 1.5% in 2005. It survived only because Rodney Hide won Epsom. In 2008 it took 3.65% and five MPs and gave National confidence and supply: Hide became Minister of Local Government and Regulatory Reform, and Heather Roy a minister outside Cabinet. Former National leader Don Brash joined ACT and took over in April 2011 when Hide stepped aside, amid internal pressure on Hide's leadership.

**The one-MP era (2011–2020).** From 2011 to 2020 ACT had a single MP, every time through Epsom, where National signalled that its voters should give ACT their electorate vote:

| Election | Leader | Party vote | Seats | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | Don Brash (John Banks led after the election) | 1.07% | 1 (Banks, Epsom) | Confidence and supply with National. Banks became Minister for Regulatory Reform and Small Business. The deal brought in charter (partnership) schools |
| 2014 | Jamie Whyte (Seymour from 3 Oct 2014) | 0.69% | 1 (Seymour, Epsom) | Confidence and supply. Seymour became Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Education (charter schools) and Regulatory Reform |
| 2017 | David Seymour | 0.50% | 1 | Opposition |
| 2020 | David Seymour | 7.58% | 10 | Opposition |
| 2023 | David Seymour | 8.64% | 11 | Coalition with National and NZ First |

- The 2011 "teapot tape" meeting between John Key and Banks in Epsom made the Epsom arrangement a national controversy. In 2014 John Key again encouraged National voters in Epsom to back Seymour, and about 60% of National voters there split their vote.
- John Banks retired as leader in 2014 to fight electoral-fraud charges over his 2010 Auckland mayoral campaign return. He was convicted in 2014, but the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction in 2015 and the Crown did not seek a retrial ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Banks_(New_Zealand_politician))).
- Leader Jamie Whyte (2014) attracted controversy over remarks on incest laws and on Māori "legal privilege". He resigned after the election.
- ACT's main achievement as a one-MP party was Seymour's **End of Life Choice Act**. It passed in 2019, was approved at the 2020 referendum and came into force on 7 November 2021.

**Breakthrough (2020).** ACT's rise to 7.6% and 10 MPs had three causes, according to analysts cited by Wikipedia. Seymour was the only MP to vote against the 2019 semi-automatic firearms ban, which drew gun owners (and firearms advocate Nicole McKee) to ACT. He was also a sharp critic of the COVID-19 response. And National was in leadership turmoil, while some NZ First voters were unhappy with Labour.

**2023 and coalition.** ACT won 8.64% and 11 seats, its best result. Brooke van Velden won Tāmaki, ACT's first electorate outside Epsom. In 2022 Seymour had said a Treaty-principles referendum would be a condition of coalition. In the end ACT signed a coalition agreement with National on 24 November 2023 that did not include a referendum (see below).

## In government, 2023–2026

**Ministers:** Seymour (Regulation; Associate Finance, Health (Pharmac) and Education; Deputy PM from 31 May 2025), Brooke van Velden (Internal Affairs; Workplace Relations and Safety), Nicole McKee (Courts; Associate Justice (firearms)), Karen Chhour (Children; Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence), Andrew Hoggard (Biosecurity; Food Safety; Associate Agriculture). Simon Court was Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Infrastructure and RMA reform.

**Main coalition wins delivered** (details and sources in the [track record](./track-record.md)):
- **Ministry for Regulation**, established 1 March 2024 and funded by abolishing the Productivity Commission.
- **Regulatory Standards Act 2025**, passed 13 November 2025 (68–55), in force 1 January 2026.
- **Charter schools return**: legislation passed 25 September 2024; 18 schools open by July 2026, against Budget 2024 funding for 50.
- **Three-strikes law reinstated** (December 2024, introduced by McKee) and an **Arms Act rewrite** (Arms Act 2026, passed 29 July 2026).
- Interest deductibility for landlords restored (80% from April 2024, 100% from April 2025), pet bonds, 90-day trials for all employers, repeal of Fair Pay Agreements, and a Reserve Bank inflation-only mandate.
- Repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act (April 2025), and a "need not race" directive for public services (September 2024).
- Deputy PM rotation: Seymour succeeded Winston Peters on 31 May 2025.

**What ACT did not get:**
- The **Treaty Principles Bill** was introduced and passed its first reading, as agreed. It drew a record 300,000 written submissions, about 90% opposed, and the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti. It was **voted down 112–11 at its second reading on 10 April 2025**, with National and NZ First voting against.
- No return of the public service to 2017 size, no abolition of "demographic" ministries, no repeal of the Zero Carbon Act, no reversal of the live-export ban, and no four-year-term referendum.
- ACT used the "agree to disagree" clause on the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill (July 2024), the scope of the firearms-registry review (May 2025) and the under-16 social media ban (August 2026). ACT also opposed the modern slavery bill (January 2026) and a gift-card expiry bill, and refused government backing for National's social-media bill in May 2025.

**Controversies (factual):**
- In June 2024 Stuff reported allegations of bullying and a "culture of fear" during ACT's 2023 campaign. The party said an independent review had been carried out and its recommendations accepted.
- The 2025 Equal Pay Amendment Act, led by Brooke van Velden as Workplace Relations Minister, passed under urgency. It raised the thresholds for pay-equity claims and discontinued the 33 claims then in progress ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Amendment_Act_2025)).
- The redesigned school lunch programme was criticised for meal quality.
- In June 2026 Porirua candidate Lyra Yan Zhang left the list after failing to declare past membership of the China Zhi Gong Party.

## Money: donations

- In 2022 ACT received over $2 million in large donations, including several rich-list donors giving $100,000 each ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/05/electoral-donations-for-2022-national-received-more-than-10-times-what-labour-got.html)).
- ACT declared about $4.3m in donations in its 2023 return, behind National's $10.4m and Labour's $4.8m ([Weekend Herald](https://www.pressreader.com/new-zealand/weekend-herald/20240504/281578065741385)).
- In the 2025 annual returns ACT overtook Labour in donations ([RNZ, 7 May 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/594551/national-tops-party-donations-list-act-overtakes-labour)).
- Wikipedia's 2026 election tracker lists about $4.79m in declared donations as of late October 2026. Donors include Nick Mowbray ($225,000), Brian Cartmell ($200,000), Greymouth Petroleum subsidiary GMP Environmental ($100,000) and Van Den Brink Karaka ($100,000). ACT reported $2.35m raised in 2026 by 24 September ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election)).

## 2026 pitch

The campaign was launched at Shed 10, Auckland, on 28 June 2026 under the theme **"Lock Labour Out, Unlock New Zealand's Potential"**. Seymour named three focuses: government waste, cutting business restrictions, and equal rights under the law ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/29-06-2026/aura-edits-and-protests-field-notes-from-the-act-partys-big-flash-rally), [speech on Scoop](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2606/S00205.htm)). Broadcaster Paul Henry is fourth on the list. Headline promises, all sourced in [`act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json) and [policies](./policies/README.md):

- **Fiscal plan (11 October 2026):** gradually raise the NZ Super age by three months a year; pause Super Fund contributions; return non-welfare spending to 2017 per-capita levels; $653m in disability-benefit savings through independent medical certification; abolish demographic ministries; cut foreign aid ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/11/act-sets-out-plan-to-raise-retirement-age-cut-debt-and-spending/)).
- Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years and introduce a training wage; no tax on KiwiSaver earnings; repeal the Zero Carbon Act and net-zero target; abolish the Climate Change Commission.
- Disestablish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are settled; entrench "equal rights" in constitutional statutes; end "race-based hiring" in the public service.
- Immigration restrictions: deport serious non-citizen offenders, a five-year benefit stand-down for new residents, a $6-a-day surcharge on temporary work visas, and abolition of the permanent-resident visa category.
- Add burglary to three strikes; a $2b National Cancer Centre (Henry); raise Pharmac's share of the health budget; let pharmacists treat more conditions; supermarket competition through a one-stop consenting body, while opposing a forced break-up.

## Coalition stance for 2026

- ACT is campaigning to re-form the National-led government and keep Labour out ("Lock Labour Out").
- Seymour defended voters' right to split their vote, after National's John Key and Christopher Luxon urged National supporters not to.
- ACT and NZ First have clashed publicly. After NZ First pledged to repeal the Regulatory Standards Act it had voted for, Seymour accused Peters of bad faith and of positioning for a deal with Labour ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_Standards_Act_2025)).

## Leaders

Roger Douglas (1994–96) · Richard Prebble (1996–2004) · Rodney Hide (2004–11) · Don Brash (2011) · John Banks (2012–14) · Jamie Whyte (2014) · David Seymour (2014–). Deputy leaders since 2017: Beth Houlbrooke (2017–20), Brooke van Velden (2020–26), Nicole McKee (2026–).

- Wikipedia, *Sixth National Government of New Zealand*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand
- Wikipedia, *Treaty Principles Bill*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_Principles_Bill; *Regulatory Standards Act 2025*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_Standards_Act_2025; *Charter schools in New Zealand*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_schools_in_New_Zealand; *End of Life Choice Act 2019*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019; *Ministry for Regulation*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_for_Regulation

# Advance New Zealand (Advance NZ) — incl. the NZ Public Party

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Deregistered** 19 August 2021 |
| **Founded** | Announced April 2020 by independent MP Jami-Lee Ross; registered 6 August 2020 |
| **Leaders** | Co-leaders Jami-Lee Ross and Billy Te Kahika (NZ Public Party), July–October 2020 |
| **Ideology** | Billed by Ross as centrist and anti-corruption; campaigned largely on COVID-19 and vaccine conspiracy claims, 5G, 1080 and opposition to lockdowns |
| **Seats** | None won (Ross lost his seat) |

## History

Jami-Lee Ross, MP for Botany, left National in 2018 after accusing leader Simon Bridges of corruption over a
$100,000 donation; he was later himself charged by the Serious Fraud Office over the donation scheme and was acquitted
at a High Court trial that began in July 2022, while three co-defendants were convicted. In July 2020 Advance merged campaigns with Billy Te Kahika's NZ Public
Party, a party known for spreading COVID-19 "plandemic" misinformation; other component parties were the NZ People's
Party, Reset NZ and Direct Democracy NZ. [1][2]

During the campaign the Speaker referred Ross to the Privileges Committee for using doctored parliamentary footage in an
advertisement, the Advertising Standards Authority ordered removal of an ad comparing COVID-19 deaths to seasonal flu,
Facebook removed the party's page for repeated COVID-19 misinformation, and the leaders held a mass rally on 12 September
2020 in defiance of distancing rules. Advance won **0.98%** (28,429). Te Kahika claimed the election was rigged; the
Public Party split from Advance on 26 October 2020 and Te Kahika shut it down in February 2021. Te Kahika was later
convicted (and discharged on appeal) of breaching COVID-19 lockdown rules. [1][3][4]

## Election results (2011–2023)

| Election | Ballot name | Party votes | Party vote % | Seats | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 | Advance NZ | 28,429 | 0.98 | 0 |  |

## MPs

None elected. Co-leader Jami-Lee Ross was the sitting (independent, ex-National) MP for Botany when he founded Advance; he chose not to defend Botany and left Parliament in 2020.

# Alliance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Registered; contesting 2026** — relaunched 2025, re-registered 5 August 2026; list of 17 |
| **Founded** | 1 December 1991 (NewLabour, Democrats/Social Credit, Mana Motuhake, Greens; Liberals joined 1992) |
| **Leaders (this period)** | Co-leaders Kay Murray (2007–15), Andrew McKenzie (2008–12), Kevin Campbell (2012–15); vacant 2015–26; **Victor Billot** (2026) |
| **Ideology** | Democratic socialism; free education and health care, full employment, progressive tax, replacing GST with a financial-transactions tax |
| **Seats** | None since 2002 (10 MPs elected in 1999; junior coalition partner to Labour 1999–2002) |
| **2026 policies** | [./policies/README.md](policies/README.md) |

## History

The Alliance was Jim Anderton's left-wing grouping that won 18% of the vote (but only two seats under first-past-the-post)
in 1993, won about 8% and ten seats in 1999 and entered coalition with Labour, introducing paid parental leave and
Kiwibank. It split in 2002 when Anderton's faction left (the Progressives), and
the rump lost all its seats. [1]

**2011–2015.** When Anderton retired from Wigram in 2011, former MP Kevin Campbell stood there (fourth, 793 votes). The
party won 0.05% (1,209 votes per the official count; Wikipedia's party article gives 1,069). In 2014 it ran no list and
one electorate candidate (Napier, 59 votes), and it was deregistered at its own request on 26 May 2015, though it never
formally dissolved. [1][2]

**Relaunch (2025–26).** In June 2025 the party announced a relaunch and stood a candidate for Christchurch City Council
(unsuccessful). It announced in January 2026 that it would stand electorate candidates nationwide. On 7 June 2026 the
**Maritime Union of New Zealand** voted to affiliate (while keeping its Labour affiliation); Billot, a former MUNZ
communications staffer, called it a "gamechanger". The party was re-registered on 5 August 2026. [1][3]

## Election results

| 2011 | 1,209 | 0.05 | 0 | Kevin Campbell 4th in Wigram |

| 2017–2023 | did not contest | — | — | deregistered 2015 |
| 2026 | — | — | — | Victor Billot |

  8 Josh Harford (Wellington North), 9 Courtney Fraser (Ilam), 10 Jesse Luke (Selwyn), 11 Joshua Moss (Palmerston North),
  12 Jen Olsen, 13 Quentin Findlay, 14 Greg Byrnes (Christchurch Central), 15–17 Peter Wilson, Cory Aitken, Brian Byas.
  Released via Scoop 7 October 2026. [4]

# Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Registered; contesting 2026** (list of 10; nine electorate candidates) |
| **Founded** | Incorporated society 11 Nov 2022; registered as a party 16 August 2023 (name used with permission of Australia's Animal Justice Party) |
| **Leaders** | Co-leaders **Robert McNeil** and **Danette Wereta** |
| **Ideology** | Animal rights, non-violence towards animals, transition to a plant-based economy, climate action |
| **Seats** | None |
| **2026 policies** | [./policies/README.md](policies/README.md) |

## History and policy

The party's 2023 platform included banning recreational fishing and hunting competitions, rodeo, horse racing, fur and
leather production and animal experimentation; supporting the greyhound-racing ban; ending intensive winter grazing
("mud farming") and factory farming; opposing 1080; a commissioner for animals; and a phased shift from animal farming
to plant-based agriculture with support for farmers. It also campaigns against the coalition government's plan to
reverse the 2023 live-export ban. [1]

policy.nz says co-leader Robert McNeil cited a lack of Green candidates in East Auckland seats and a perception that the
Greens compromise as reasons for founding it. [2]

The party ran 17 candidates in 2023 and won **0.18%** (5,018 votes); it came fourth in the 2023 Port Waikato
by-election. An August 2025 poll put it at 1% for the first time. In the 2025 local elections it stood unsuccessfully
for the Auckland and Hamilton mayoralties and other seats. [1]

  (Takanini), 9 Caitlin Grattan (Mount Maunganui), 10 Sam Connely (Tauranga). [4]

# Ban 1080 Party

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Deregistered** at its own request on 28 February 2018 |
| **Founded** | 2014 by Bill Wallace; registered 8 August 2014 |
| **Leaders** | Co-leaders Bill Wallace and Mike Downard |
| **Ideology** | Single issue: end aerial drops of sodium fluoroacetate (1080) poison; "people not poison" targeted pest control |

## History

The party wanted the Department of Conservation's aerial 1080 programme stopped immediately and replaced with
species-specific protection plans and targeted pest control. Its best candidate result was Pete Salter's 6.5% (fourth)
in West Coast-Tasman in 2014. Police visited party officials in 2015 during the investigation into threats to
contaminate infant formula with 1080; the threats were found to be unrelated to the party. After the 2017 result it
deregistered, and many supporters moved to the [Outdoors Party](../nz-outdoors-freedom/README.md). [1][2]

# Conservative Party NZ (formerly Conservative Party, New Conservative, New Conservatives)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Registered; contesting 2026** (party list of 8, five electorate candidates) |
| **Founded** | 3 August 2011 by Colin Craig; registered 6 October 2011 |
| **Names** | Conservative Party (2011–17) → New Conservative (Nov 2017) → New Conservatives (2023) → **Conservative Party NZ** (name change notified by the Electoral Commission 28 Jan 2026) |
| **Leaders** | Colin Craig (2011–15); vacant (2015–17); Leighton Baker (2017–20); Elliot Ikilei (Nov–Dec 2020); Helen Houghton & Ted Johnston co-leaders (2021–23); **Helen Houghton** (2023–) |
| **Ideology** | Social conservatism, lower taxes, anti-abortion/anti-euthanasia; described by some opponents as far-right, while the party says it has moved to a "more centrist" position |
| **Best result** | 3.97% (2014) — the highest result of any party never to win a seat in this period |
| **2026 policies** | [./policies/README.md](policies/README.md) (maintained by another agent) |

> This is one continuous party (same registration) under several names, so there is no separate `new-conservative`
> folder. It is unrelated to the earlier "New Zealand Conservative Party". [1]

## History

### Colin Craig era (2011–2015)
Businessman Colin Craig, who had organised a 2009 protest march and polled third (8.7%) in the 2010 Auckland mayoralty,
launched the party on 3 August 2011. It absorbed members of the Kiwi Party (Larry Baldock) and New Citizen Party,
spent NZ$1.88 million in 2011 — the second-highest of any party, mostly Craig's own money — and campaigned on raising
the drinking age to 21, parental notification for abortion, repealing the "anti-smacking" law and opposing asset
sales. It won **2.65%**; Craig came second in Rodney. [1]

In 2014 there was speculation that National would stand aside in a North Shore seat for Craig, but on 28 July 2014 John
Key said Murray McCully would not step aside in East Coast Bays. Craig won a High Court injunction to be included in a
minor-party TV debate. Days before the election press secretary Rachel MacGregor resigned, citing Craig's behaviour. The
party won **3.97%** (95,598 votes), short of the 5% threshold — the largest single-party "wasted" vote at any election from 2011
to 2023 (NZ First's 75,020 in 2020 and TOP's 63,344 in 2023 were the next largest). [1][2][5]

Craig resigned on 19 June 2015 amid the MacGregor dispute; the board collapsed in recriminations. In 2016 a jury found
Craig had defamed Taxpayers' Union director Jordan Williams (awarding $1.27m, later set aside by the judge as excessive).
A police investigation into 2014 campaign spending cleared Craig. He left the party in October 2016. [1][3]

### Leighton Baker era (2017–2020)
Under Leighton Baker the party fell to **0.24%** in 2017, renamed itself New Conservative in November 2017, and rebuilt
around free speech, opposition to abortion and euthanasia law reform, opposition to the UN migration compact and to the
post-Christchurch gun reforms. It rose to **1.48%** (42,613 votes) in 2020 after unsuccessfully suing TVNZ to join a
minor-party debate. The board replaced Baker with Elliot Ikilei in November 2020; Ikilei quit on 31 December 2020. [1]
Baker later founded the short-lived [Leighton Baker Party](../leighton-baker/README.md).

### Houghton era (2021– )
Christchurch teacher Helen Houghton and lawyer Ted Johnston became interim co-leaders in October 2021, saying they
wanted to appeal to centrist voters; Johnston said the party no longer sought to abolish the Māori seats, ease gun laws
or introduce forced prison labour. Johnston left in September 2023 to form the Unity Party (allied with the Democratic
Alliance). The 2023 "Family Builder" policy ($9.1 billion in year one: first $20,000 of income tax-free, child tax
credits, income splitting, funding parents rather than ECE centres) was questioned by researcher Max Rashbrooke. The
party won **0.16%**, its worst result. In 2026 it reverted to the Conservative name. [1][4]

## MPs

  5 Marie Drury (Northcote), 6 Paul Deacon, 7 Jonathan Marshall, 8 Amy Turner (Banks Peninsula). Released via Scoop on

  euthanasia"; policy.nz lists 2025 donations of $9,519.73 and polling "<0.5%". Broadcasting allocation $78,887

# Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (Rōpū Kākāriki)

> Profile current to **23 October 2026**, 15 days before the 7 November 2026 general election.
> See also: [Track record: promises vs delivery](./track-record.md) · [2026 policies](./policies/README.md) ·
> [Promise tracker data](../../data/promises/green.json) · [People](./people/)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Founded** | 26 May 1990 (successor to the Values Party, founded 1972); part of the Alliance 1991–97 |
| **Co-leaders** | Marama Davidson (since 8 April 2018) and Chlöe Swarbrick (since 10 March 2024) |
| **Position** | Green politics, social democracy; usually described as centre-left to left |
| **Seats (54th Parliament)** | 15 of 123 (11.6% party vote in 2023, the party's best result; 3 electorates and 12 list seats) |
| **In government** | Confidence & supply 1999–2002 (no ministers); **confidence & supply 2017–20** (3 ministers outside Cabinet and 1 under-secretary); **cooperation agreement 2020–23** (2 ministers outside Cabinet) |
| **2026 slogan** | "For All of Us" |
| **International** | Global Greens; Asia Pacific Greens Federation |

## 1. Summary

The Greens are New Zealand's third-largest party. They have passed the 5% threshold at every election since leaving the Alliance in 1997. Their weakest result was 5.3% in 2005 and their best was 11.6% in 2023. They have helped form three Labour-led governments. Under MMP they have never joined, or given confidence and supply to, a National-led government. The Greens hold four values: ecological wisdom, social justice, grassroots democracy and non-violence. They also accept Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the country's founding document.

The Greens have had two spells with ministers, in 2017–23. Their biggest achievement was the **Zero Carbon Act (2019)**, along with a cannabis referendum and a range of climate, housing and welfare measures. The cost was a run of compromises their own members disliked. Examples are the 2018 vote for NZ First's waka-jumping law and the 2020 Green School grant (see the [track record](./track-record.md)).

In opposition since 2023, the Greens have:
- polled at record highs, up to 16% in 2026;
- moved their economic message towards cost of living and wealth taxes;
- been hit by a run of MP scandals and departures, more than any other caucus this term.

## 2. History

| Period | Key events |
|---|---|
| 1972–1990 | The **Values Party** contests elections. The Green Party is formed in 1990. |
| 1991–1997 | Part of the **Alliance**. Green MPs first enter Parliament in 1996 on the Alliance list. |
| 1999–2005 | Stand alone. In 1999 Jeanette Fitzsimons wins Coromandel and the Greens give confidence and supply to the Labour–Alliance government (1999–2002). Co-leader Rod Donald dies in November 2005. |
| 2008–2014 | 2008: 6.72%, 9 MPs. A policy memorandum of understanding with John Key's National government follows (2009; it lapsed in 2011). 2011: 11.06%, 14 MPs. 2014: 10.70%, 14 MPs. Russel Norman (co-leader 2006–15) campaigns successfully against mining on Schedule 4 conservation land and leads the citizens-initiated referendum against asset sales. |
| 2015–2017 | James Shaw becomes co-leader (May 2015). Labour and the Greens campaign under a memorandum of understanding. In July 2017 co-leader **Metiria Turei** tells the party AGM she had committed benefit fraud in the 1990s, to highlight welfare failures. Support briefly hits 15%. MPs Kennedy Graham and David Clendon quit the caucus on 7–8 August. Turei resigns on **9 August 2017**, and the party falls to about 4% in one poll. |
| 2017 election | 6.27%, 8 MPs. Chlöe Swarbrick (aged 23) and Golriz Ghahraman (the first refugee MP) enter Parliament. NZ First chooses Labour, and the Greens sign a **confidence and supply agreement** with Labour (October 2017). |
| 2017–2020 | First time Greens hold ministerial roles (see §5). Marama Davidson becomes female co-leader on 8 April 2018. |
| 2020 election | 7.86%, 10 MPs. Swarbrick wins **Auckland Central**, only the second Green electorate win. Labour wins a majority but offers a **cooperation agreement**, which 85% of Green delegates accept (31 October 2020). |
| 2020–2023 | Internal discontent: some members called the party "Labour's little helper". Leadership challenges against Shaw in 2021 (he won 116–4) and July 2022 (he was not reconfirmed, then re-elected unopposed with 97% in September 2022). In May 2022 the party changes its rules: one co-leader must be a woman, the other can be of any gender, and at least one must be Māori. Elizabeth Kerekere quits in May 2023 (see §6). |
| 2023 election | **11.60%, 15 MPs**, the party's best result. It wins three electorates: Auckland Central (Swarbrick), Wellington Central (Tamatha Paul) and Rongotai (Julie Anne Genter). The party goes into opposition. |
| 2023–2026 | Shaw resigns as co-leader and Swarbrick is elected unopposed (169–0) on 10 March 2024. A run of caucus departures and scandals follows (§6). In 2025 the party releases an "alternative budget" ($8b over four years, a Ministry of Green Works). By September 2026 it is polling at record highs. |

## 3. Values: the Charter

The Green Charter has four principles:
- **ecological wisdom**
- **social justice**
- **appropriate decision-making** (grassroots democracy; the wording follows secondary sources, which call this principle "grassroots democracy")
- **non-violence**

The party also accepts Te Tiriti o Waitangi as New Zealand's founding document and recognises Māori as tangata whenua. Members disagree about whether the Charter calls for eco-socialism or a broader "ecological economics". This shows up as a long-running tension between the party's pragmatic wing (Norman's "green growth", Shaw's 2017 Budget Responsibility Rules) and its left wing (the GreenLeft network, and former MPs Sue Bradford and Catherine Delahunty). In 2025–26 The Spinoff and other commentators described the economic platform as a "dramatic break" with the Shaw era.

## 4. Co-leadership model and co-leaders

The party has six equal office-holders: two parliamentary co-leaders, two party co-convenors and two policy co-convenors. **Since May 2022** the co-leaders must be one woman and one person of any gender, and at least one must be Māori. Before that the rule was one man and one woman. Members' delegates confirm the co-leaders every year at the AGM. A 25% vote to reopen nominations triggers a contest, which is what happened to Shaw in July 2022.

| Co-leader | From | To | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rod Donald | 21 May 1995 | 6 Nov 2005 | Died in office |
| Jeanette Fitzsimons | 21 May 1995 | 30 May 2009 | |
| Russel Norman | 3 Jun 2006 | 30 May 2015 | Announced his resignation in Jan 2015; later led Greenpeace NZ |
| Metiria Turei | 30 May 2009 | **9 Aug 2017** | Resigned during the 2017 campaign after the benefit-fraud admission |
| James Shaw | 30 May 2015 | 10 Mar 2024 | Sole leader Aug 2017–Apr 2018; Climate Change Minister 2017–23; left Parliament May 2024 |
| Marama Davidson | 8 Apr 2018 | incumbent | Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence 2020–23; breast-cancer treatment June 2024–Feb 2025 |
| Chlöe Swarbrick | 10 Mar 2024 | incumbent | MP for Auckland Central since 2020 |

## 5. In government, 2017–2023

**Confidence & supply (October 2017 to 2020).** The Greens supported the Labour–NZ First coalition from outside it.

| Minister | Role |
|---|---|
| James Shaw | Minister for Climate Change; Minister of Statistics; Associate Minister of Finance |
| Julie Anne Genter | Minister for Women; Associate Minister of Health; Associate Minister of Transport |
| Eugenie Sage | Minister of Conservation; Minister for Land Information; Associate Minister for the Environment |
| Jan Logie | Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Justice (domestic and sexual violence) |

Items in the agreement included:
- a Zero Carbon Act and an independent Climate Change Commission;
- a cannabis referendum by 2020;
- a "Green Transport Card";
- rail and cycling investment, and light rail to Auckland Airport;
- more funding for the Department of Conservation;
- an end to "excessive" benefit sanctions;
- closing the gender pay gap;
- a rent-to-own scheme within KiwiBuild;
- re-establishing the Mental Health Commission.

The agreement also obliged the Greens to let the Labour–NZ First coalition deal be implemented. That is why they voted for the waka-jumping bill.

**Cooperation agreement (31 October 2020 to 2023).** Labour governed alone with a majority. Two Green ministers sat outside Cabinet:
- James Shaw: Minister for Climate Change, and Associate Minister for the Environment (biodiversity);
- Marama Davidson: Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence, and Associate Minister of Housing (homelessness).

The Greens also got one select-committee chair and one deputy-chair role. Former MPs Russel Norman, Sue Bradford and Catherine Delahunty said the deal gave the party too little leverage.

What the Greens actually delivered in these terms, and where they fell short, is assessed in the [track record](./track-record.md).

## 6. Caucus departures and discipline, 2023–2026

The Greens have lost or disciplined more MPs this term than any other party. In date order, with sources:

- **Elizabeth Kerekere** (list MP 2020–23). In April 2023 the party opened an investigation after she called Swarbrick a "crybaby" in a leaked group chat. RNZ then reported bullying allegations from at least seven current and former staff. She **resigned from the party on 5 May 2023** before the process ended and sat as an independent. In her valedictory speech she accused Shaw and Davidson of an "epic failure of leadership" and of denying her natural justice. Māori, Pasifika and Rainbow members defended her.
- **Golriz Ghahraman**. Accused of shoplifting from Auckland and Wellington boutiques in late 2023. She stood aside on 10 January 2024 and **resigned from Parliament on 16 January 2024**, citing an "extreme stress response". She pleaded guilty to four charges (goods worth $9,978 in total) and was convicted and fined $1,600 in June 2024. Her bid for a discharge without conviction was refused, and she lost her appeal in October 2024. Celia Wade-Brown replaced her.
- **Fa'anānā Efeso Collins** died on 21 February 2024 during a charity run. Lawrence Xu-Nan replaced him.
- **James Shaw** retired in May 2024. Francisco Hernandez replaced him.
- **Darleen Tana** (list MP from 2023). Suspended on 15 March 2024 over migrant-exploitation allegations at her husband's e-bike business. An independent investigation by barrister Rachel Burt found she played a major role in the business and knew of the complaints before she became a candidate. She **resigned from the party on 8 July 2024** but refused to leave Parliament. Swarbrick said her conduct was "completely at odds with our party's values". The Greens then used the **Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act 2018**, the waka-jumping law they had long opposed, to remove her. 185 delegates agreed by consensus on 17 October 2024, and the Speaker declared her seat vacant on **22 October 2024**. This was the first expulsion under the 2018 Act. Three senior Pasifika members resigned in protest, saying Tana and Kerekere had been mistreated. Benjamin Doyle replaced her.
- **Julie Anne Genter**. On 1 May 2024 she crossed the chamber and shouted "Read the report!" at minister Matt Doocey. On **1 August 2024 she was found in contempt**, censured and ordered to apologise. The party called her conduct "unacceptable". Wellington business owners also made separate complaints about confrontations over cycleways.
- **Benjamin Doyle** (Parliament's first non-binary MP, from November 2024). In early 2025 they became the target of a campaign over a 2023 Instagram post. Doyle reported death threats against them and their child, and Police charged more than 10 people. Doyle **resigned effective 3 October 2025**, citing safety, and called Parliament "hostile and toxic". Mike Davidson replaced them.
- **Tamatha Paul** (MP for Wellington Central). In March 2025 she said "police beat patrols" made some communities feel less safe, and in a TikTok video she said most prisoners were jailed for non-violent, poverty-related offences. She later said she regretted the prison comment. Labour's Hipkins called her police comments "ill-informed… stupid" and the Prime Minister also criticised them. She stood by her police comments. She is No. 4 on the 2026 list.
- **Chlöe Swarbrick**:
  - December 2023: refused, then gave, an apology for calling a Prime Ministerial statement a "demonstrable lie".
  - 12–13 August 2025: ordered out for saying "If we find 6 of 68 Government MPs with a spine…" during a Palestine debate. She refused to apologise and was "named", which meant a suspension with docked pay.
  - 4 August 2026: ejected for accusing the Speaker of "double standards" over Winston Peters telling Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to "go back to your own country".
- **Marama Davidson**. In 2023, as a minister, she said at a protest that "white cis men" cause violence, then clarified the remark. She was ejected in June 2023 for accusing ACT of racist questioning. She was treated for breast cancer from June 2024 and returned at Waitangi in February 2025.
- **NZ First remarks about migrant-background Green MPs**, 2025–26. Targets included Ricardo Menéndez March ("sending Mexicans home"), Xu-Nan, Hernandez and Teanau Tuiono. The Prime Minister called Peters' July 2026 remark racist but kept him as Foreign Minister.
- **October 2026: Mongrel Mob meeting**. Green MP Hūhana Lyndon and Te Pāti Māori MPs met Mongrel Mob members at a South Auckland election meeting and were photographed with them. National attacked the meeting, and Newsroom said it could put the Greens' poll gains at risk. The Greens were "unapologetic".

Not every episode above involves wrongdoing. Doyle, Collins and the NZ First remarks do not. They are listed because together they shaped the caucus this term. Integrity issues measured against Green values are discussed in the [track record](./track-record.md#5-actions-vs-values).

## 9. 2026 polling

In polls from August to October 2026 the Greens ranged from about **12% to 16%**. 1News–Verian had them at 16% on 23–27 September 2026, which it called their best result ever. The last 1News–Verian poll before this snapshot (15–19 October) also had them on 16%. Other recent results:
- Freshwater Strategy (9–19 October): 14.3%
- Taxpayers' Union–Curia (1–5 October): 13.3%
- RNZ–Reid Research (24 September to 1 October): 14.8%

On these numbers the Greens would get roughly 17–20 seats (our estimate). With Labour, the left bloc is roughly level with the governing coalition, and the Opportunity Party is often described as the possible kingmaker. Full series: [`data/polls-2026.json`](../../data/polls-2026.json).

## 10. 2026 pitch and headline promises

The campaign slogan is **"For All of Us"**. The Greens' manifesto was launched at its AGM in Auckland in July 2026. It combines climate and environment policy with cost-of-living policies funded by taxing the very wealthy and corporations to pay for a "floor" of food, shelter and jobs. Headline commitments:

- **Tax**:
  - 2.5% tax on net wealth over $10m, plus an inheritance tax on large estates;
  - 33% company rate for the biggest corporations;
  - new top bracket above $160,000;
  - first $10,000 of income tax-free.
- **Housing**: cap annual rent increases at 2%; a rental warrant of fitness; tens of thousands of new public homes.
- **Cost of living**: "KiwiMart", a government-owned supermarket chain; restore and expand free school lunches; fare-free public transport for young people, disabled people and Community Services Card holders, with a $2 adult fare cap.
- **Energy and climate**: "Kiwipower", a Crown entity investing in renewables; "electrify everything"; repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act and revoke the mining consents granted under it; a one-year pause on new AI data centres.
- **Water and oceans** ("Drink, Swim, Fish"): phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, reduce stock numbers, protect 30% of the oceans.
- **Work**: restore pay equity ($4.5b for care workers); automatic union membership; abolish the training wage.
- **Transport**: $4b for intercity rail; removing Auckland level crossings ($2.5–3.5b).
- **Te Tiriti and te reo**: $200m for te reo Māori; a $2.4b marae resilience trust; entrench the Māori seats.
- **Democracy**: a $30,000 donation cap and no corporate donations; a lobbying register.
- **Foreign policy**: recognise Palestine and sanction Israel.

The full list is in [./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md).

## 11. Coalition stance

The Greens will only support a **Labour-led government**. In February 2026 at Waitangi, Hipkins, Swarbrick and Davidson announced that Labour and the Greens would work together during the campaign and in government. Te Pāti Māori is asking its voters to give their party vote to Labour or the Greens, so a centre-left government would probably need Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, and possibly the Opportunity Party.

Some sticking points are already public:
- Labour has ruled out supporting Te Pāti Māori's Te Tiriti Commission, which the Greens say fits their own policy.
- In 2020 Ardern ruled out a wealth tax.
- Labour did not adopt rent caps in 2017–23.

No sources found so far report any Green 2026 bottom lines.

# Internet Party (and Internet MANA, 2014)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Unregistered / dormant** — deregistered 12 June 2018 (membership below 500); has not contested any election since 2017 and has not announced dissolution |
| **Founded** | Announced 15 January 2014 by Kim Dotcom; registered 13 May 2014 |
| **Leaders** | Laila Harré (2014); Suzie Dawson (Feb 2017 – Apr 2018) |
| **Ideology** | Internet freedom, privacy, copyright reform, cheaper broadband; anti-mass-surveillance |
| **Seats** | None |

## History

Kim Dotcom — the Megaupload founder whose Auckland home was raided in January 2012 at the request of US authorities —
announced the Internet Party in January 2014. It signed up members through a phone app and was registered on 13 May
2014. Dotcom gave it NZ$3.5 million, described as the largest personal contribution to a New Zealand party on record.
Former Alliance MP and minister Laila Harré was chosen as leader. [1]

**Internet MANA (2014).** In May 2014 the party agreed an alliance with Hone Harawira's [Mana Movement](../mana/README.md):
the combined "Internet Party and MANA Movement" (registered 24 July 2014) contested the party vote, with Mana taking list
places 1, 3 and 4 and the Internet Party 2, 5 and 6. The strategy depended on Harawira holding Te Tai Tokerau, which would
have let Internet MANA bring in list MPs below 5%. On election night Harawira lost to Labour's Kelvin Davis (8,969 to
9,712 on election-night figures) and Internet MANA's 1.42% won no seats. Dotcom said: "the brand Kim Dotcom was poison
for what we were trying to achieve." The alliance was dissolved on 13 December 2014 and Harré resigned. [1][2][3]

**2017.** Activist Suzie Dawson, then living in Russia, became leader in February 2017. The party ran eight list
candidates and won 499 party votes (0.02%), the lowest of any registered party. Dawson stepped down in April 2018 (no
longer eligible, having lived abroad three years) and the party was deregistered on 12 June 2018. It obtained a
conditional 2020 broadcasting allocation ($41,457) but did not re-register or stand. [1]

| 2014 | 34,094 (Internet MANA) | 1.42 | 0 | joint list with Mana |
| 2017 | 499 | 0.02 | 0 | standalone |

Source: official results as tabulated in the Wikipedia election articles (`raw/minor-parties/results.json`). [4]

## Policy (2014 launch agenda)

Unlimited high-speed internet 50% cheaper; a second submarine cable; high-tech jobs; restricting government
surveillance; reviewing the TPPA; copyright reform; clean energy; reducing inequality. [1]

## Notable events

# New Zealand Labour Party (Rōpū Reipa o Aotearoa)

> New Zealand's oldest current political party (founded 1916); Wikipedia's infobox describes it as social-democratic and centre-left.
> **Leader:** [Chris Hipkins](./people/chris-hipkins/) (since 22 Jan 2023) · **Deputy:** [Carmel Sepuloni](./people/carmel-sepuloni/) (since 7 Nov 2023) ·
> **Finance spokesperson:** [Barbara Edmonds](./people/barbara-edmonds/) · **2026 slogan:** "Better Starts Now" ·
> **Status (Oct 2026):** Official Opposition, 34 MPs · **Last in government:** 2017–2023
>
> See also: [Track record & promise tracker](./track-record.md) · [2026 policies](./policies/README.md) · [Promise data (JSON)](../../data/promises/labour.json)

*Compiled 23 October 2026. Every factual claim is linked to a source; where sources disagree or we could not verify something, that is said explicitly.*

---

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 7 July 1916, by trade unions and socialist groups ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)) |
| Ideology | Social democracy; constitution still states democratic-socialist principles; in practice pragmatic centre-left ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)) |
| Times in government | 6 (1935–49, 1957–60, 1972–75, 1984–90, 1999–2008, 2017–23) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) |
| Current MPs | 34 (17 electorate, 17 list) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) |
| 2023 result | 26.91% party vote, 34 seats — down from 50.01% / 65 seats in 2020 |
| 2026 polling | ~27–31% in October 2026 polls, down from ~34–37% in the first half of 2026 (see below) |
| Donations | $3.27m declared electoral donations 2025–Oct 2026 (third behind National and ACT) |
| Party colour | Red |

---

## History

**Origins (1916–1935).** Labour was formed in 1916 as the political wing of the union movement. Its early leaders (Harry Holland, Peter Fraser, Bob Semple, Paddy Webb) opposed WWI conscription and some were jailed. It won 8 seats in 1919 and became the official Opposition in 1926; policies such as the "usehold" (state leasehold) land policy were dropped during the 1920s ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**First Labour Government (1935–1949)** under Michael Joseph Savage and Peter Fraser built the modern welfare state (state housing, social security, free health care). **Second (1957–60)** under Walter Nash and **Third (1972–75)** under Norman Kirk/Bill Rowling were single-term governments.

**Fourth Labour Government (1984–1990)** under David Lange and Finance Minister Roger Douglas carried out wide-ranging market liberalisation ("Rogernomics") — deregulation, corporatisation and privatisation — which split the party and its union base, and also made New Zealand nuclear-free. Membership collapsed in the 1980s–90s ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**Fifth Labour Government (1999–2008)** under Helen Clark (three election wins) governed in MMP coalitions/support arrangements (Alliance, Progressives, United Future, NZ First, Greens). It introduced KiwiSaver, Working for Families, the NZ Super Fund, Kiwibank, interest-free student loans and NCEA; the 2004 foreshore and seabed controversy led to the breakaway Māori Party ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**Opposition (2008–2017)** — four leaders in nine years (Goff, Shearer, Cunliffe, Little). The 2014 result (25.13%) was Labour's worst since 1922. Policies run in 2011 and 2014 — a capital gains tax, raising the pension age to 67, NZ Power, KiwiAssure — were all dropped by Andrew Little after 2014 (see [track record](./track-record.md#1-opposition-era-promises-2011--2014)). With Labour polling at 24%, Little stood down on 1 August 2017 and Jacinda Ardern took over seven weeks before the election ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

**Sixth Labour Government (2017–2023)** — see [Government periods](#government-periods-2008-2026) below.

**Opposition again (2023–2026).** Hipkins was re-elected leader after the 2023 defeat; veterans Grant Robertson, Kelvin Davis and Rino Tirikatene (2024) and David Parker (2025) left Parliament. Labour called for recognition of Palestinian statehood (April 2024) and Hipkins said a Labour government would not be part of AUKUS (December 2024). Several Labour members' bills passed with cross-party support (e.g. Camilla Belich's wage-theft and pay-secrecy bills, Deborah Russell's divorce-wait exemption for family-violence victims) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party); [54th Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament)).

## Ideology and principles

Labour's 1916 objective was "the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange"; the socialist objective was dropped in 1951. The current constitution lists democratic-socialist principles — management of natural resources for all, equal access regardless of wealth, co-operation in economic relations "to ensure a just distribution of wealth", the right to work, people "more important than property", **honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi**, international co-operation, and equality regardless of race, sex, sexuality, gender identity, age, religion or disability. Observers describe its policy as pragmatic social democracy with social-liberal positions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

Core voter base today: young people, urban workers, public servants, and Māori and Pasifika communities ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

## Organisation and union links

- **Structure:** electorate branches and special branches (Māori, Pasifika, women, rainbow, university, etc.) → Labour Electorate Committees → six regional conferences → **Annual Conference** (called Congress in election years), the supreme body. The **New Zealand Council** is the governing executive; a **Policy Council** elected each term writes the platform and manifesto ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).
- **Caucus elects Cabinet:** unusually, Labour's caucus — not the leader — elects its ministers ([Wikipedia: Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).
- **Leadership rules (2021):** a candidate needs two-thirds of caucus; failing that, an electoral college of caucus 40% / members 40% / **affiliated unions 20%** decides ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).
- **Affiliated unions:** 11 affiliated unions in 2023, paying a levy by membership; the CTU president speaks at the annual conference ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)). Union influence over leadership votes is a recurring criticism. Policy closely aligned with unions in government: Fair Pay Agreements, doubled sick leave, pay equity settlements, repeal of 90-day trials for larger firms.
- **Young Labour** is the youth wing. The party's handling of 2018 Young Labour camp assaults and of 2019 complaints against a staffer drew heavy criticism; party president Nigel Haworth resigned in 2019 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand)).
- **Party presidents** (recent): Andrew Little (2009–11), Moira Coatsworth (2011–15), Nigel Haworth (2015–19), Claire Szabó (2019–22), Jill Day (2022–). *Dates from Wikipedia's list of presidents; not independently re-verified.*

Key events of the Sixth Labour Government: Christchurch mosque attacks and semi-automatic firearms ban (2019); Whakaari eruption (2019); COVID-19 elimination strategy, wage subsidy and border closure (2020–21); abandonment of elimination after Delta and the 2022 Parliament occupation; 7.3% inflation (June 2022, a 32-year high) ([1News](https://1news.co.nz/2022/07/18/inflation-rises-to-73-a-32-year-high/)); Ardern's resignation and Hipkins' "policy bonfire" (2023); Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle (2023). Ministerial resignations or sackings included Clare Curran, Meka Whaitiri, Phil Twyford, David Clark, Stuart Nash, Kiri Allan, and [Michael Wood](./people/michael-wood/) (2023) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

## Donations and funding

- **$3,273,137.93** in declared electoral donations from 1 January 2025 to late October 2026 — behind National ($8.47m) and ACT ($4.79m). It includes $125,000 from the Mills Family Trust and $219,178 from the estate of Murray George Jones. In 2026 itself (to 24 September) Labour declared $869,896 from 15 donors ([Wikipedia: 2026 election — Fundraising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election), citing [RNZ's donations tracker](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/647946/political-donations-tracker-act-gets-another-dollar225-000-and-overall-parties-total-exceeds-2023-campaign)).
- policy.nz lists Labour's **2025** donations as $2,403,241.93 ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)).
- Affiliated unions pay levies to the party (see above).
- In 2020 the Serious Fraud Office investigated donations to Labour from two Chinese businessmen around the 2017 election; the party said it co-operated ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

## 2026 pitch and headline promises

Slogan **"Better Starts Now"**, launched 24 August 2026 ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/24/labour-reveals-its-2026-election-campaign-slogan/)). Labour is campaigning on cost of living, health access, jobs and "changing the government"; National has focused its attack on the capital gains tax. Headline commitments (full list and verbatim documents in [policies/](./policies/README.md)):

- **Capital gains tax** of 28% on residential and commercial property, excluding the family home and farms, from July 2027 — funding **up to three free GP visits a year** (Medicard), free maternity scans and free cervical screening ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/577021/labour-to-campaign-on-narrow-capital-gains-tax-no-wealth-tax)).
- **NZ Future Fund** to invest in infrastructure and NZ firms (details withheld until after the election) ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/10/20/nz-future-fund-labour-reveals-first-major-policy-for-next-election/); [NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-admits-it-will-not-release-cornerstone-policy-costing-and-job-modelling-until-after-the-election-blames-treaty-of-waitangi-concerns/QNGXJK4SHZFOJB52WFCVHPLR4E/)).
- **$20/week public transport fare cap** in the three main cities ($10 elsewhere) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360990643/labour-reveals-public-transport-fare-cap-long-awaited-election-policy)).
- **Fiscal strategy:** surplus by 2029/30, net debt ~20% of GDP, an independent budget office ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1081146/labour-releases-fiscal-strategy-promises-to-slash-debt)).
- **$4b for 6,000+ social housing places, school and hospital repairs** ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1552827/labour-pledges-4-billion-for-state-houses-school-repairs-and-hospitals)); **10% student-loan write-off** ($583.4m) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-kicks-off-campaign-after-national-hammers-home-tax-attack/JJ6SXVR3HJH2RB7BF4567UTSDI/)); **restore pay equity** and a $2.5b pay rise for care and support workers ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1718141/labour-releases-its-fiscal-plan-promises-pay-rise-for-care-and-support-workers)).
- **Cost of living / competition:** split supermarket wholesale from retail, ban price gouging, a "fair go" law on hidden fees, airline and bank competition measures ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1478631/labour-proposes-splitting-foodstuffs-and-woolworths-from-their-wholesale-arms)).
- **KiwiSaver:** compulsory employer contributions, 6% minimum ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1356180/labour-to-make-employer-contributions-to-kiwisaver-compulsory-if-elected)).
- **Reversals of coalition policy:** repeal the Regulatory Standards Act within 100 days; scrap youth boot camps; pause the NCEA/curriculum overhaul; restore school boards' Treaty obligations; restore locally made school lunches and rural school bus routes.
- **Rule-outs:** no GST rise in 2027, oppose fuel excise rises, no change to landlord interest deductibility.
- **Foreign policy:** recognise Palestine, sanctions on Israel, stay out of AUKUS, aid towards 0.7% of GDP ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/1528401/labour-sums-up-its-foreign-policy-approach-as-independent-principled-and-unafraid)).

How these compare with Labour's past delivery: [track record §9](./track-record.md#9-what-the-record-suggests-for-2026-promises).

# Mana Movement (Mana Party)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Deregistered** at its own request in May 2021 (3 May per Wikipedia; Electoral Commission notice dated 5 May 2021). Not contesting 2026. |
| **Founded** | Launched 30 April 2011; registered 24 June 2011 |
| **Leader** | Hone Harawira (2011–2021) |
| **Ideology** | Left-wing; tino rangatiratanga / Māori rights; "a political waka for all peoples" focused on "the poor, the powerless and the dispossessed" |
| **Seats** | 1 (Te Tai Tokerau), June 2011 – Sept 2014 |
| **Track record** | [track-record.md](track-record.md) · [promise data](../../data/promises/mana.json) |

## History

**Formation (2011).** Hone Harawira, MP for Te Tai Tokerau since 2005, left the Māori Party in February 2011 after its
disciplinary committee recommended his expulsion; he had opposed the party's stance on the foreshore and seabed
replacement law and its relationship with National. He launched the Mana Party on 30 April 2011 with backing from
activist John Minto and former Green MPs Nándor Tánczos and Sue Bradford, plus Annette Sykes and Matt McCarten. [1][2]
He resigned his seat to force a by-election (25 June 2011), which he won for Mana with a 1,117-vote majority, then held
the seat at the November 2011 general election (majority 1,165 over Labour's Kelvin Davis). [1][3][4]

**Opposition MP, 2011–14.** Harawira's member's bill to fund breakfast and lunch in decile 1–2 schools (the "Feed the
Kids" bill) was drawn from the ballot on 8 November 2012. Mana activists were prominent in protests against state-asset
sales, the TPPA and state-house demolitions in Glen Innes (Harawira was arrested there in October 2012). Mana's Te
Hamua Nikora came second (26.1%) in the 2013 Ikaroa-Rāwhiti by-election and John Minto ran for Auckland mayor in 2013
on free public transport. [1][3]

**Internet MANA (2014).** In May 2014 Mana formed an electoral alliance with Kim Dotcom's Internet Party — see
[Internet Party](../internet-party/README.md). Sue Bradford resigned in protest. The joint list won 1.42% but
Harawira lost Te Tai Tokerau to Kelvin Davis by 743 votes after National and NZ First leaders urged supporters to vote
tactically for Davis, so the alliance won no seats. It was dissolved on 13 December 2014. [1][3][5]

**2017 and after.** Under a memorandum of understanding with the Māori Party, Mana stood only in Te Tai Tokerau (and
Māngere); Harawira lost again to Davis (12,673 to 7,866) and Mana won 0.14%. It did not contest 2020, endorsing the
Māori Party, and was deregistered at its own request in 2021. [1][3]

## Election results

| Election | Party votes | Party vote % | Seats | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 by-election (Te Tai Tokerau) | — | — | 1 | Harawira won, majority 1,117 |
| 2011 | 24,168 | 1.08 | **1** (Te Tai Tokerau) | electorate seat only |
| 2014 | 34,094 (as Internet MANA) | 1.42 | 0 | Harawira lost by 743 |
| 2017 | 3,642 | 0.14 | 0 | |
| 2020 | did not stand | — | — | endorsed Māori Party |

Party-vote figures: official results as tabulated by Wikipedia (`raw/minor-parties/results.json`). [4]

## MPs

- **Hone Harawira** — MP for Te Tai Tokerau 2005–2014 (Māori Party 2005–11, independent Feb–June 2011, Mana
  2011–14). No person folder exists in this archive. [3]

## Notable controversies (factual)

- Harawira's 2011 by-election was criticised by Labour, the Greens and the Māori Party as a costly "publicity stunt"
  (estimated $500,000). [1]
- In September 2012 Harawira described National's Māori MPs on Facebook using a racial slur ("house niggers") and
  defended the remark; in June 2017 he called for the death penalty for Chinese methamphetamine importers. [3]
- The Internet MANA alliance with Kim Dotcom (whose money funded it) was controversial on the left; Dotcom said on
  election night that "the brand Kim Dotcom was poison". [1][5]

## Current status

Deregistered (2021). Harawira led Far North COVID-19 checkpoints in 2020–21. [1][3]

# New Zealand National Party (Rōpū Nāhinara o Aotearoa)

National is New Zealand's main centre-right party. It is the senior partner in the current coalition government with ACT and NZ First, and it has led a government six times since 1936, more often than any other party. Its 2026 slogan is **"Fixing the Basics. Building the Future."**

- **Track record**: what National promised versus what it delivered, 2008–2026, in [track-record.md](track-record.md) (82 promises assessed). The underlying data is in [`data/promises/national.json`](../../data/promises/national.json).
- **2026 policies**: every policy, with full source texts, in [policies/README.md](policies/README.md).
- **Candidates and MPs**: [people/](people/).

*Compiled 23 October 2026, ahead of the 7 November 2026 election. Every figure links to a source; downloaded copies are in `raw/record/national/`.*

## Quick facts

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 13–14 May 1936 in Wellington, from a merger of the United (Liberal) and Reform parties ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)) |
| Leader | [Christopher Luxon](people/christopher-luxon/), leader since 30 Nov 2021 and Prime Minister since 27 Nov 2023 |
| Deputy leader | [Nicola Willis](people/nicola-willis/), deputy since 30 Nov 2021 and Minister of Finance |
| Party president | Sylvia Wood, since August 2022 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/sylvia-wood-elected-national-party-president/ZVWXEVMLI64MG4D6QJ5YYXBLJI/)) |
| Position and ideology | Centre-right. Conservatism and liberalism, a "broad church" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)) |
| International affiliation | International Democracy Union; Asia Pacific Democracy Union |
| Headquarters | 41 Pipitea Street, Thorndon, Wellington |
| MPs (54th Parliament) | 49, of whom 43 hold electorates (48 at the 2023 election, plus the Port Waikato by-election) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz)) |
| 2023 result | 38.06% of the party vote, 48 seats, largest party |
| 2026 polling | policy.nz average 30.8%; latest polls range from about 26% to 32% (see [Polling 2026](#polling-2026)) |
| Donations declared | 2025: $6,275,234.46, the most of any party. 2024: $4,889,538.20. 2023 (election year): about $10.35m ([1News/RNZ](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/05/07/national-tops-party-donations-list-act-overtakes-labour/); [Electoral Commission](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/2025-annual-party-returns)) |
| Youth wing / other wings | Young Nationals; Bluegreens (environment); National with Pride (LGBTQ) |
| Website | <https://www.national.org.nz> |

## History

- **Formation (1936).** United, which drew its support from city business, and Reform, which drew on farmers, had governed together in 1931–35 and lost heavily to Labour in 1935. They merged in May 1936 to oppose Labour. National's first leader was Adam Hamilton, followed by Sidney Holland in 1940 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)).
- **First government (1949–57)**, under Holland and then Holyoake. It kept Labour's welfare state, and defeated the unions in the 1951 waterfront dispute.
- **Second government (1960–72)**, under Holyoake and then Marshall. This was a 12-year period of stable, broadly consensual government.
- **Third government (1975–84)**, under Robert Muldoon. It was economically interventionist: "Think Big" energy projects, and a wage and price freeze. It lost the 1984 snap election.
- **Fourth government (1990–99)**, under Bolger and then Shipley. It continued the free-market reforms begun by Labour's Roger Douglas: Ruth Richardson's "Ruthanasia" budgets, and the Employment Contracts Act. It formed the first MMP coalition, with NZ First in 1996, which collapsed in 1998. Jenny Shipley was New Zealand's first female Prime Minister (1997).
- **Opposition (1999–2008).** National's worst result came in 2002 (20.9%) under Bill English. Under Don Brash it recovered to 39.1% in 2005, campaigning on tax cuts and the "Orewa" race-relations speech. John Key became leader in 2006.
- **Fifth government (2008–17)**, under Key and then English. This was a minority government, with confidence and supply from ACT, United Future and the Māori Party. It steered the country through the global financial crisis and the Canterbury earthquakes, carried out a GST/income-tax switch, sold minority stakes in state energy companies, held the flag referendums, and returned the budget to surplus from 2014/15. See [Wikipedia: Fifth National Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand).
- **Opposition (2017–23).** In 2017 National won 44.4%, the largest party, but NZ First chose Labour. Four leaders followed in four years: Bridges, Muller, Collins and Luxon. The party slumped to 25.6% in 2020, its second-worst result ever.
- **Sixth government (2023–present)**, under Luxon. New Zealand's first three-party coalition under MMP, with ACT and NZ First. See [Wikipedia: Sixth National Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) and the [track record](track-record.md).

## Ideology and factions

National's constitution lists these values: loyalty to country and Sovereign; "recognition of the Treaty of Waitangi as the founding document of New Zealand"; national and personal security; equal citizenship and opportunity; individual freedom and choice; personal responsibility; competitive enterprise; limited government; strong families; and sustainable development ([Wikipedia summary of party principles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)).

National has been characterised as a **"broad church"** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party), citing political scientist Jack Vowles):
- a **conservative** wing, with rural, provincial and socially conservative members;
- a **liberal** wing, both economic (classical-liberal) and social;
- smaller **populist** and **libertarian** tendencies.

The party has a free conscience vote on moral issues. Its MPs split on same-sex marriage, and mostly opposed the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. Wikipedia says the Key-English government (2008–17) "took a relatively centrist position" (citing The Spinoff, 2016). The Luxon government's programme has included welfare sanctions, deregulation, the reversal of Labour-era Treaty-related and shared Māori–Crown governance measures (which the coalition parties call "co-governance"), and a return to oil and gas exploration; what it promised and delivered is assessed in the [track record](track-record.md).

## Organisation

- National has two parts. The party organisation (members, run by an elected Board of Directors and a president) and the parliamentary caucus, which elects the leader.
- The annual conference sets policy and elects board members. Each electorate committee sends delegates.
- Membership was about 200,000 in the mid-1970s and had fallen below 30,000 by the early 2000s ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)). No recent membership figure has been published.
- National has led New Zealand party fundraising in every recent year (see Quick facts). In 2023 its disclosed donors included Graeme Hart's Rank Group ($400,000) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/election-2023/498251/billionaire-graeme-hart-s-700k-in-donations-to-right-wing-parties)). Donations under the $5,000 disclosure threshold are not itemised ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/08-05-2026/three-and-a-bit-years-and-50m-of-political-donations-visualised)).

## Periods in government and arrangements

**Fifth National Government (19 Nov 2008 – 26 Oct 2017)**
- National governed as a minority, with confidence-and-supply agreements with ACT, United Future and the Māori Party in all three terms. A memorandum of understanding with the Greens in 2009 lapsed in 2011.
- Support-party leaders held ministerial posts outside Cabinet: Rodney Hide and Heather Roy (ACT), Tariana Turia and Pita Sharples (Māori Party), and Peter Dunne (United Future).
- Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand).

**Sixth National Government (27 Nov 2023 – present)**
- **Structure.** National signed two separate coalition agreements, one with ACT and one with NZ First.
- **Deputy Prime Minister.** The role was split: Winston Peters held it until 31 May 2025, then David Seymour.
- **Cabinet.** 13 National ministers, 3 from ACT and 3 from NZ First.
- **What National gave up.** Its foreign-buyer tax and its plan to raise the super age to 67, both conceded to NZ First.
- **What National took on from its partners:**
  - from ACT: faster restoration of interest deductibility, the Treaty Principles Bill to select committee, the Regulatory Standards Bill, and charter schools;
  - from NZ First: the Regional Infrastructure Fund, the English-language law, an expanded COVID inquiry, and moving fees-free to the final year.
- **"Agree to disagree".** Clauses in the agreements let partners vote against government bills. They have been used several times: ACT on the Fair Digital News Bargaining bill and the under-16 social media ban; NZ First on new residence pathways and the India free trade agreement.
- Sources: [1News coalition explainer](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/11/25/nationals-coalition-deals-which-policies-made-the-cut/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand).

## The 2026 campaign: pitch and headline promises

National launched its campaign in Auckland on 27 September 2026. Luxon's "personal commitment" list ([National](https://www.national.org.nz/news/260927-christopherluxon-1)) was:

1. Economic growth "that delivers new jobs and higher wages"
2. **No new taxes**
3. **Compulsory KiwiSaver**, with higher contributions and a **$1,500 Baby Boost**
4. **Paid parental leave** extended from 26 to 30 weeks
5. Better school results, by **replacing NCEA**, with regular assessment and "teaching the basics brilliantly"
6. "Tougher consequences for criminals" (its words), and more police patrols
7. Faster healthcare and more medicines, on top of 33 new cancer medicines already funded
8. Better infrastructure: Roads of National Significance, new classrooms, and new and upgraded hospitals
9. A better deal at the supermarket, through more competition (including structural separation of Foodstuffs)
10. **Books in surplus**: an OBEGALx surplus in 2028/29, debt below 40% of GDP, and spending moving towards 30% of GDP

Later campaign releases added more ([plan for young adults](https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261023-young-adults); [Kiwi kids](https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261021-christopherluxon); [retirement](https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261022-retirement)):
- a lower student-loan repayment rate (10%);
- wider 5%-deposit First Home Loans;
- a ban on social media for under-16s;
- keeping students at school to the end of Year 11;
- no screens in early childhood education;
- 20% of the Housing Flexible Fund ring-fenced for seniors' housing;
- an 0800 Seniors helpline;
- employer KiwiSaver contributions for over-65s from July 2027.

The pitch rests on National's first-term record and on attacking the alternative:
- **The record National claims**: tax relief "for the first time in 14 years"; 2.6% growth; ram raids down; school phone ban.
- **The attack**: a "Labour–Greens–Te Pāti Māori–Opportunity" coalition with "at least nine new taxes".
- **Official statistics and forecasts** (assessed promise by promise in the [track record](track-record.md)): annual CPI inflation fell to 2.2% in the September 2024 quarter and was 3.7% in the year to September 2026 ([interest.co.nz, 22 Oct 2026](https://www.interest.co.nz/economy/140742/annual-inflation-hits-37-september-quarter-petrol-continuing-lead-way-followed)); unemployment was 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter, an 11-year high ([1News, 5 Aug 2026](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/05/nzs-unemployment-rate-hits-11-year-high-in-june-quarter/)); and Treasury's pre-election update forecast a return to surplus (on the government's OBEGALx measure) in 2028/29, with net debt peaking at 43.9% of GDP ([RNZ on PREFU 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1647005/treasury-gives-willis-pre-election-boost-as-surplus-forecast-improves)).

Full list of every 2026 policy, with source documents: **[policies/README.md](policies/README.md)**.

## Coalition stance and bottom lines for 2026

- **Preferred partners: ACT and NZ First.** National's message is "three more years to finish the job" with the current arrangement ([National](https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261022-nicolawillis)).
- **Opportunity: ruled out.** Luxon ruled out working with Opportunity (TOP) on 27 July 2026, citing its tax plans, including a land tax and a universal basic income: "When you want to spend more, tax more, borrow more — we ain't doing business with you". His office confirmed this was a rule-out ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/07/27/luxon-appears-to-rule-out-national-working-with-opportunity-party/)).
- **Te Pāti Māori.** In 2023 Luxon ruled out any coalition with Te Pāti Māori ([interest.co.nz](https://www.interest.co.nz/public-policy/121148/christopher-luxon-fends-friendly-fire-act-shutting-down-possibility-forming)). This archive found no 2026 statement reversing that. National's campaign material treats Te Pāti Māori as part of the opposing bloc.
- **Labour.** National does not present a grand coalition as an option. It has, however, passed legislation with Labour's votes: the India free trade agreement, the National Infrastructure Plan, the first readings of the RMA replacement bills, and a co-sponsored modern-slavery bill.
- **Stated bottom line: no new taxes.** This is the main condition National itself has set out ([National: no new taxes](policies/documents/policy-no-new-taxes.md)).
- **Friction with its current partners:**
  - NZ First has vowed to repeal ACT's Regulatory Standards Act;
  - NZ First opposed the India free trade agreement;
  - both ACT and NZ First oppose National's under-16 social media ban ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand)).
