# New Zealand First (NZ First)

> Party founded in 1993 by **Winston Peters**, who has led it ever since; Wikipedia's infobox lists its ideology as right-wing populism, nationalism and social conservatism, and its economic policy is interventionist (see the ideology row below). It has been a junior partner in the National-led coalition since November 2023.
> **Leader:** Winston Peters: Minister of Foreign Affairs; Deputy Prime Minister 27 Nov 2023 – 31 May 2025; Minister for Rail. **Deputy leader:** [Shane Jones](./people/shane-jones/README.md) (elected by caucus 17 Sept 2025): Minister for Regional Development, Resources, Oceans and Fisheries.

- 2026 policies: **[./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md)**
- Track record (promises vs delivery, reliability, alignment): **[./track-record.md](./track-record.md)**
- Promise data: [`data/promises/nz-first.json`](../../data/promises/nz-first.json)

## Quick facts

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 18 July 1993 by Winston Peters, after he fell out with National over its economic policies (he was sacked from Cabinet in 1991 and told he could not stand again for National) |
| Ideology | Variously described as populist, right-wing populist, nationalist, centrist, socially conservative; economically interventionist and protectionist; supports binding referendums; restrictive on immigration; focused on pensioners. One academic (Todd Donovan, 2020) argues "radical right" is a misclassification |
| Seats (54th Parliament) | 8 of 123, all list MPs |
| 2023 party vote | 6.08% (173,425 votes) |
| 2026 polling | Roughly 7.5–15% across 2026 polls; 8–12% in October 2026 polls |
| Governments it has enabled | National 1996–98 (coalition); Labour 2005–08 (confidence and supply); Labour 2017–20 (coalition); National 2023– (coalition) |

## History: the kingmaker

- **1993–1996.** Peters won the 1993 Tauranga by-election as an independent. NZ First won 8.4% and two seats in 1993. In 1996, the first MMP election, it took 13% and 17 seats, including all five Māori seats (the "Tight Five").
- **1996: coalition with National.** Peters campaigned strongly against National, and many voters expected a deal with Labour. He chose National, becoming Deputy PM and Treasurer. The coalition broke up in August 1998 when Jenny Shipley sacked him over the sale of Wellington Airport. Half the caucus split off to keep supporting National, and in 1999 the party fell to 4%.
- **2002–2005.** It recovered to 10.4% and 13 seats in 2002, campaigning on immigration, Treaty costs and crime. In 2005 it fell to 5.72%, and Peters lost Tauranga. During the campaign he had spoken of staying on the cross-benches and rejecting the "baubles of office", but he then took Foreign Affairs (outside Cabinet) in a confidence-and-supply deal with Helen Clark's Labour. That deal produced the **SuperGold Card** (launched 2007).
- **2008: out.** The party was hit by a donations controversy involving Owen Glenn, the Vela family and Bob Jones. The Serious Fraud Office and Police found no wrongdoing, but Parliament's Privileges Committee censured Peters for knowingly misleading Parliament by not declaring a donation. John Key ruled NZ First out, and it won 4% and no seats.
- **2011–2017: return.** It came back with 6.59% (8 MPs) in 2011, helped by the "teapot tape" affair, and won 8.66% (11 MPs) in 2014. Peters won the 2015 Northland by-election.
- **2017: kingmaker again.** With 7.2% and 9 MPs, NZ First negotiated with both major parties and on 19 October 2017 chose **Labour** (with Green confidence and supply). Peters became Deputy PM and Foreign Minister; Shane Jones ran the $3b Provincial Growth Fund; Ron Mark was Defence Minister; Tracey Martin held Children and Internal Affairs.
- **2020: out again.** It won 2.6% and lost every seat. That year the **NZ First Foundation** case broke (below).
- **2023: return and coalition with National.** Peters ruled out Labour before the election and campaigned on "Take our country back". NZ First won 6.08% and 8 list MPs, and on 24 November 2023 signed a coalition agreement with National. That made it part of New Zealand's first three-party coalition under MMP, alongside ACT.

## The NZ First Foundation case (2020–2022)

- In February 2020 the SFO began investigating the NZ First Foundation. The allegation was that donations (about half a million dollars, 2017–19) had been channelled through it to pay party expenses without being declared as party donations.
- The SFO charged two people in September 2020. At the 2022 trial the Crown alleged that $746,881 had been obtained by deceiving donors, the party secretary and the Electoral Commission.
- **Both defendants were acquitted on 22 July 2022**, and their names are permanently suppressed. Peters was not charged and has always denied wrongdoing.
- Labour's Justice Minister then announced tighter donation laws. Third-party entities were brought within the definition of donations, and the disclosure threshold was lowered.

(Source: [Wikipedia: New Zealand First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First))

## In government, 2023–2026

**Ministers:** Peters (Foreign Affairs, Racing; later Rail; Deputy PM until 31 May 2025); Shane Jones (Regional Development, Resources, Oceans and Fisheries); Casey Costello (Customs, Seniors); Mark Patterson (Rural Communities, Associate Agriculture); Jenny Marcroft (Under-Secretary, Media and Communications).

**Main coalition wins delivered** (details and sources in the [track record](./track-record.md)):
- NZ Super age kept at 65, and no foreign buyer tax.
- A **$1.2b Regional Infrastructure Fund**: $1,070m committed, $858m approved, but only $153m paid out at 31 July 2026.
- **English Language Act 2026**, passed 30 July 2026 with Labour's support; English-first names for government agencies.
- **Māori ward referendums** restored: in October 2025, 24 of 42 councils voted to remove their wards.
- A broadened **COVID-19 inquiry** (phase-two report released 10 March 2026).
- Te Aka Whai Ora abolished; smokefree generation law repealed; relationships and sexuality education guidelines withdrawn.
- **Fast-track Approvals Act 2024**, and the offshore oil and gas exploration ban reversed (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).
- As Rail Minister, Peters handled the aftermath of the cancelled iReX mega-ferries. Total cost of the cancelled project: $671m. Replacement ferries were ordered at a fixed price of US$335m, for service from 2029 ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/08/15/how-much-it-cost-to-cancel-irex-ferry-contract/)).

**Blocking, permitting and "agree to disagree":**
- **Permitted then blocked ACT's Treaty Principles Bill:** voted for it at first reading (Nov 2024), as agreed, then against it at second reading (Apr 2025).
- **Voted for the Regulatory Standards Act** at its third reading (13 Nov 2025), then pledged a week later to repeal it.
- **Invoked "agree to disagree"** over:
  - the scope of the COVID inquiry (mid-2024);
  - new work-residency pathways (Sept 2025);
  - the India free trade agreement (Dec 2025; NZ First voted against its legislation in 2026, which passed with Labour support);
  - the under-16 social media ban (Aug 2026).
- Opposed the Gene Technology Bill unless it was changed (Nov 2025), and opposed legislation allowing advertising on certain public holidays (Oct 2025).

**Controversies (factual):**
- In March 2024 Peters compared co-governance to Nazi race ideology; Luxon called the remarks unhelpful.
- In April 2024 Shane Jones attacked the Waitangi Tribunal's summons process.
- In 2023, media reported conspiracy-linked views held by several NZ First candidates.
- On 29 July 2026 Peters told Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan in Parliament to "go back to your own country" (details and sources in [his profile](./people/winston-peters/README.md#controversies)). On 10 August Labour formally ruled out working with NZ First, citing "overt racism" ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/10/labour-rules-out-nz-first-hipkins-says-caucus-call-was-unanimous/)).

## Money: donations

As of late October 2026, Wikipedia's 2026 election tracker lists about $2.11m in declared donations. Donors include Brian Cartmell ($204,999), Sir Peter Vela ($150,000), GMP Environmental ($100,000) and Michael Sullivan ($50,000). NZ First reported $753,000 raised in 2026 by 24 September ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Zealand_general_election)). For past donations controversies, see 2008 and the Foundation case above.

## 2026 pitch and bottom lines

Peters' State of the Nation speech (Tauranga, 22 March 2026) and the campaign that followed focused on cost of living, national identity, "anti-co-governance" and immigration. Former MPs Alfred Ngaro (NewZeal), Michael Laws, Ron Mark and Harete Hipango are on the 2026 list. Headline promises, all sourced in [`nz-first.json`](../../data/promises/nz-first.json) and [policies](./policies/README.md):

- **A binding referendum on the Māori seats** (revived from 2017). Also: abolish the Waitangi Tribunal and replace it with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission; disestablish Auckland's Independent Māori Statutory Board.
- **Citizens-only voting**; **NZ Super only for citizens from 2029**; social housing for citizens first; a ten-year benefit stand-down for migrants; tighter visas; a two-year amnesty for overstayers who leave voluntarily.
- **Superannuation at 65** stays a defining commitment (it was secured in the 2023 deal).
- Split power companies' generation and retail arms; split Foodstuffs into two co-operatives; buy back **BNZ** and merge it with Kiwibank; KiwiSaver enrolment at birth; a $5,000-a-year "Kiwi Kids Grant".
- **Repeal the Regulatory Standards Act**; amend the fast-track regime; a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point; a 20% company tax rate for small businesses.

NZ First has not published a formal list of 2026 coalition "bottom lines". Earlier campaigns treated the Māori-seat referendum (2017) and super at 65 as conditions.

## Coalition stance for 2026

- Peters ruled out Labour well before the campaign. In August 2026 Labour ruled out NZ First, saying the caucus decision was unanimous ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/10/labour-rules-out-nz-first-hipkins-says-caucus-call-was-unanimous/)). That leaves a renewed National-led arrangement as NZ First's only realistic route to government.
- Peters defended strategic vote-splitting when National urged its voters not to split, accusing National of "desperation".
- Relations with ACT are tense: Seymour accused NZ First of bad faith over its pledge to repeal the Regulatory Standards Act.

## History

**2023.** NZ Loyal pledged to pull New Zealand out of the UN, WEF and WHO, "establish" a written constitution, impose
an immigration moratorium, oppose "race-based policies", and investigate the Reserve Bank, the "Green Agenda" and the
media. Gunn's health statements repeated false claims about vaccines (she called the COVID-19 response a
"mini-holocaust") and promoted alternative therapies. [1]

The party won **1.21%** (34,478 votes) and none of its 33 electorate candidates won. Because it missed the nomination
deadline for most of its intended 15-person list, its official list held only three names (one of whom left the party);
the High Court refused to let it add names after the deadline ("If you leave it to the last minute and something goes
wrong, the responsibility falls squarely on the party"). Had it passed 5%, most of its seats would have been left
empty. [1]

**Deregistration and split (2024–25).** The party's registration was cancelled at its own request in July 2024; Gunn
then applied to trademark the name personally. Kelvyn Alp of the far-right platform Counterspin Media accused her of
shutting the party down unconstitutionally; a new board elected Alp leader in November 2024. Alp polled 26 votes (last)
in the 2025 Tāmaki Makaurau by-election. Gunn calls Alp's party a "fake NZ Loyal". [1]

**2026.** The party applied to re-register in June 2026 and was registered in August (its logo was refused). [1][2]
policy.nz notes Alp's "background in conspiracy media, an armed militia that has targeted bankers, and ... legal battles
regarding the distribution of videos from the Christchurch Mosque attacks". [3]

## History

The Outdoors Party stood four candidates in 2017 (0.06%). After the Ban 1080 Party deregistered, many of its
supporters joined, and anti-1080 lawyer **Sue Grey** became co-leader around the start of 2020. During 2020 it called the
COVID-19 lockdown "cruel and unreasonable" and compared the government to the Nazi Party; an Auckland rally in June 2020
featured 9/11 "false flag", flat-earth and anti-5G claims and the harassment of a young Asian woman (Grey said those
involved were not party members). Several candidates defected before the 2020 election (0.11%). [1]

It renamed itself NZ Outdoors & Freedom in April 2022. Grey won 1,030 votes (4th) in the 2022 Tauranga by-election.
In May 2023 it joined Brian Tamaki's [Freedoms NZ](../freedoms-nz/README.md) umbrella, Grey becoming co-leader with
Tamaki; the party vote in 2023 was therefore cast for Freedoms NZ (0.34%), while Grey stood for Outdoors & Freedom in
West Coast-Tasman (7th of 9). After Freedoms NZ deregistered in May 2025 the party continued on its own under Grey. [1][2]

In the 2026 campaign, a group of the party's anti-vaccination activists confronted Labour MP Ayesha Verrall at a
Wadestown candidates' meeting on 8 September; former ACT marketing director John Ansell reportedly accused her of mass
murder while livestreaming. [3]

# Opportunity Party (formerly The Opportunities Party, TOP)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status (Oct 2026)** | **Registered; contesting 2026** — 40-person list, ~40 electorate candidates. Polling 4.8–8% in October 2026, i.e. around the 5% threshold. |
| **Founded** | Launched 4 November 2016 by Gareth Morgan; registered 6 March 2017 |
| **Leaders** | Gareth Morgan (2016–17); Geoff Simmons (interim 2018, leader Dec 2018 – Nov 2020); Shai Navot (interim 2020–22); Raf Manji (Jan 2022 – Dec 2023); **Qiulae Wong** (Nov 2025 – ) |
| **Ideology** | Radical centrism / "evidence-based policy"; open to working with either Labour or National |
| **Best result** | 2.44% (2017) |
| **Seats** | None in Parliament; one local seat (Featherston Community Board, 2022) |
| **2026 policies** | [./policies/README.md](policies/README.md) (maintained by another agent) |

## History

**Gareth Morgan (2016–17).** Economist and philanthropist Gareth Morgan launched TOP in November 2016 as a party of
"evidence-based policy" in the political centre, intended to be able to work with either side. Chief of staff Geoff Simmons came third (4.56%) in the February 2017 Mount Albert by-election. In
the 2017 campaign TOP unsuccessfully sued TVNZ to join the debates, and Morgan drew criticism for calling Jacinda
Ardern "lipstick on a pig" and for remarks about the death of her cat; when candidate Jenny Condie criticised the
party culture, Morgan told her to resign. TOP won **2.44%** (63,261 votes) — the best result of any party outside
Parliament that year. Morgan stood down in December 2017, and in July 2018 briefly announced the party would deregister
before reversing course. [1][2]

**Geoff Simmons (2018–20).** Simmons was elected leader in December 2018 and relaunched the brand in October 2019
(UBI, environment, housing, "break the Labour/National duopoly"). TOP targeted Ōhāriu (Jessica Hammond Doube, third with
4,443 votes); Simmons came fourth in Rongotai. Result **1.51%** (43,449). Simmons resigned in November 2020. [1][3]

**Raf Manji (2022–23).** Former Christchurch city councillor Raf Manji — who had run second as an independent in Ilam in
2017 — became leader on 27 January 2022. TOP won its first elected office (Featherston Community Board) in October
2022. Its 2023 strategy was to win **Ilam**: Manji came second with 10,863 votes to National's Hamish Campbell (18,693).
Party vote **2.22%** (63,344). Manji resigned in December 2023; in August 2025 the party advertised the leader's job on
SEEK. [1][4][5]

**Qiulae Wong and the "Opportunity" rebrand (2025–26).** In November 2025 the party chose Qiulae "Q" Wong — formerly a
sustainable-business adviser at KPMG and NZ director of B Lab — as leader and rebranded as the Opportunity Party (the
Electoral Commission notified the name change in January 2026). [1][6]

## 2026 campaign summary

- **Pitch:** a means-tested **citizen's income** (about $370/week for almost all adults, not available above
  $350,000 income) replacing most benefits *and* NZ Superannuation, funded by a **land value tax**; compulsory
  KiwiSaver; **citizens' assemblies** ("Citizen's Voice"); a ban on **bottom trawling**; competition reforms and a
  stronger Commerce Commission; forgiving student-loan interest to draw emigrants home; lobbying regulation (register,
  one-year cooling-off) and a **$30,000 per-donor cap**; a methane emissions trading scheme and $5 billion for climate
  adaptation. On 30 September Wong named five "non-negotiables": a ten-year health plan, lobbying reform, a bottom-trawling
  ban, attacking monopolies/duopolies, and stronger climate commitments. [1][7][8]
- **Coalition stance:** open to either side, negotiating first with the largest party; Wong later said TOP would not
  support a government with Winston Peters as foreign minister. On **27 July 2026 National ruled out working with
  Opportunity** ("We wouldn't be in business with people who want to increase taxes" — Christopher Luxon). [1][9]
- **Polling:** TOP polled above 5% for the first time in 2026, peaking at 9.5% (Roy Morgan, August). October 2026
  polls: 7% and 8% (1 News–Verian), 5.4% (Freshwater Strategy; Anacta), 4.8% (Taxpayers' Union–Curia). It was the only
  extra-parliamentary party to qualify for TVNZ's multi-party debate. A Talbot Mills analysis (Jul–Aug 2026) found
  roughly a third of its supporters came from the left, a third from the right and a quarter had voted TOP in 2023. [1][10]
- **Money:** $671,061 in declared donations 2025–Oct 2026 (incl. $180,000 from Alan Wilderland, $100,000 from Brian
  Cartmell, $50,000 from Phillip Mills); broadcasting allocation $114,179 (amended to $118,755). [11]
- **List (top 10 of 40):** 1 Qiulae Wong (Mount Albert), 2 Daniel Eb (Kaipara ki Mahurangi), 3 Jessica Hammond
  (Wellington North), 4 Kayla Kingdon-Bebb (Wellington Bays), 5 Eden Skipper (Christchurch Central), 6 Jodie Kuntzsch
  (Nelson), 7 Sarah Lucas (New Plymouth), 8 David Bainbridge-Zafar (Dunedin), 9 Holly Knill (North Shore), 10 Pāpā
  Wharewera (Waiariki). Announced 31 July 2026. [12] People: [Qiulae Wong](people/qiulae-wong/),
  [Jessica Hammond](people/jessica-hammond/), [Daniel Eb](people/daniel-eb/).
- Full policy detail: [policies/README.md](policies/README.md).

## Election results

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2020 | 43,449 | 1.51 | 0 | Geoff Simmons; Ōhāriu focus |

## Notable events / controversies

## History

New Zealand's third party from the 1950s to the 1980s, Social Credit was part of the Alliance from 1991 to 2002 and
briefly of the Progressive Coalition, then re-established itself as an independent party. In this archive's period it
was a fringe party: 0.08% in 2011, 0.07% in 2014, 0.03% in 2017 and 0.05% under the restored Social Credit name in 2020.
In 2021 it opposed COVID-19 vaccine mandates. After deregistration its president Gloria Bruni said it intended to
rebrand to avoid comparison with China's "social credit system". [1][2]

Historically the movement faced accusations of antisemitism stemming from founder C. H. Douglas's views; Te Ara and
Paul Spoonley describe this as ending by the 1970s–1984 under Bruce Beetham. [1]

# Te Pāti Māori (the Māori Party)

> Profile current to **23 October 2026**, 15 days before the 7 November 2026 general election.
> See also: [Track record: promises vs delivery](./track-record.md) · [2026 policies](./policies/README.md) ·
> [Promise tracker data](../../data/promises/te-pati-maori.json) · [People](./people/)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Founded** | 7 July 2004, as "the Māori Party", after the foreshore and seabed controversy. Renamed **Te Pāti Māori** with the Electoral Commission on 12 July 2023. |
| **Co-leaders** | Debbie Ngarewa-Packer (since 15 April 2020) and Rawiri Waititi (since 28 October 2020) |
| **President** | John Tamihere (since 2022) |
| **Position** | Indigenous rights, tino rangatiratanga, a Te Tiriti-centred platform. Centrist while it supported National (2008–17); described as left or progressive since 2020. |
| **Seats (54th Parliament)** | 6 electorate seats won in 2023, creating a 2-seat overhang. 4 MPs in caucus in October 2026 after the 2025 expulsions. |
| **In government** | Confidence and supply to the **National-led governments of 2008, 2011 and 2014**, with ministers outside Cabinet |
| **2026 strategy** | Contesting the 7 Māori electorates only. Asking supporters to give their electorate vote to Te Pāti Māori and their party vote to Labour or the Greens. |

## 1. Summary

Te Pāti Māori is the only party built entirely around Māori political self-determination. Its career has had three
phases:

1. **Founding and early years (2004–08).** Tariana Turia left Labour over the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 and won the
   by-election that followed. The party won 4 Māori seats in 2005.
2. **Inside the tent with National (2008–17).** The party had confidence-and-supply "relationship accords" and
   ministers outside Cabinet: Turia, Pita Sharples and Te Ururoa Flavell. It won Whānau Ora, the replacement of the
   2004 Act, support for UNDRIP, a constitutional review, tobacco control and a new Māori language law. Its vote fell
   steadily (2.39% → 1.43% → 1.32% → 1.18%) and it lost all its seats in 2017. Metro and others called this a backlash
   against propping up National.
3. **Revival (2020–26).** Under Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi the party returned in 2020 and won a record
   6 seats in 2023. In opposition it has relied on protest, from the Treaty Principles Bill haka to nationwide hīkoi.
   It has also faced serious problems:
   - Parliament's harshest-ever privileges suspensions (2025);
   - repeated questions about party finances and data use linked to organisations led by its president;
   - a 2025 civil war that ended with two MPs expelled. The High Court later found one expulsion unlawful.

## 2. History and leadership

| Co-leader | From | To | Seat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tariana Turia | 7 Jul 2004 | 1 Nov 2014 | Te Tai Hauāuru |
| Pita Sharples | 7 Jul 2004 | 13 Jul 2013 | Tāmaki Makaurau |
| Te Ururoa Flavell | 13 Jul 2013 | 19 Jul 2018 | Waiariki (lost seat in 2017) |
| Marama Fox | 1 Nov 2014 | 5 Sep 2018 | List (2014–17) |
| *(vacant)* | 2018 | 2020 | Party outside Parliament |
| John Tamihere | 15 Apr 2020 | 28 Oct 2020 | Lost in Tāmaki Makaurau in 2020; party president since 2022 |
| **Debbie Ngarewa-Packer** | 15 Apr 2020 | incumbent | List MP 2020–23; Te Tai Hauāuru since 2023 |
| **Rawiri Waititi** | 28 Oct 2020 | incumbent | Waiariki since 2020 |

The constitution requires two co-leaders, one male and one female, drawn first from the MPs.
Presidents: Whatarangi Winiata (2004–09), Pem Bird (2010–13), Naida Glavish (2013–16), Tuku Morgan (2016–17), Che
Wilson (2018–22), John Tamihere (2022–).

### Timeline
- **2004**: Turia resigns from Labour and Parliament over the Foreshore and Seabed Act. She wins the July by-election
  for the new party.
- **2005**: 2.12%, 4 electorates (Turia, Sharples, Hone Harawira, Flavell), creating a 1-seat overhang. The party
  stays in opposition.
- **2008**: 2.39%, 5 electorates (Rahui Katene wins Te Tai Tonga), creating a 2-seat overhang. Confidence and supply
  agreement with National (16 November 2008). Sharples becomes Minister of Māori Affairs; Turia becomes Minister for the
  Community and Voluntary Sector and later Minister for Whānau Ora.
- **2011**: Harawira leaves the party in February after clashing over its support for National and for the
  replacement foreshore law, and forms Mana. The party
  falls to 1.43% and 3 seats, with a 1-seat overhang, and signs a second agreement with National.
- **2014**: Turia and Sharples retire. 1.32%: Flavell holds Waiariki and Marama Fox enters as the party's first list
  MP. Third agreement; Flavell becomes Minister for Māori Development and for Whānau Ora.
- **2017**: Electoral pact with Mana: the party stands aside in Te Tai Tokerau. **Labour wins all 7 Māori seats.** The
  Māori Party gets 1.18% and is out of Parliament. Fox says Māori had "gone back like a beaten wife to the abuser".
- **2020**: Tamihere and Ngarewa-Packer become co-leaders. Waititi wins Waiariki by 836 votes. On 1.17%, the party
  gets 2 MPs. Waititi replaces Tamihere as co-leader.
- **2020–23**:
  - the party is referred to Police over late donation disclosures (see §5);
  - it walks out over speaking rights and calls for "divorce" from the monarchy;
  - it petitions to rename the country Aotearoa (70,000+ signatures);
  - Meka Whaitiri defects from Labour (May 2023); the co-leaders are ejected for the haka welcoming her;
  - name change to Te Pāti Māori (July 2023).
- **2023**: **3.08%, 6 electorates** (Waiariki, Te Tai Hauāuru, Hauraki-Waikato, Tāmaki Makaurau, Te Tai Tokerau, Te
  Tai Tonga), creating a 2-seat overhang (123 MPs). This is the party's best result. **Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke**, aged
  21, unseats Nanaia Mahuta. Takutai Tarsh Kemp wins Tāmaki Makaurau by 42 votes. Whaitiri loses Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.
- **2023–26**: in opposition (§4–§6).

## 3. The 2008–2017 support deals: what the party gained

The 2008 confidence-and-supply agreement, announced 16 November 2008, committed National to:
- set up a group to consider constitutional issues, including Māori representation;
- not remove the Māori seats "without the consent of the Māori people" (entrenchment was shelved);
- review the Foreshore and Seabed Act and repeal it if necessary;
- appoint Sharples and Turia as ministers outside Cabinet.

What followed across the three terms:

| Gain | Year | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **Whānau Ora** | 2010 (expanded 2011, 2014) | Delivered. It became the party's signature programme, with three commissioning agencies from 2014. Contracts were re-tendered in 2025. |
| **UNDRIP endorsed** | 20 April 2010 | Delivered, as a non-binding statement, announced by Sharples at the UN |
| **Foreshore and Seabed Act repealed** and replaced by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 | 2011 | Delivered as a compromise. Turia called it "drafted by politics, rather than what is fair and moral". Harawira quit over it. The 2025 coalition amendment tightened it again. |
| **Constitutional review** | from 2011 | Delivered as a process; no major constitutional change followed |
| **Smokefree 2025**, tobacco excise rises, plain packaging (Turia) | 2011 onward | Delivered |
| **Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016** (Te Mātāwai) | 2016 | Delivered under Flavell |
| **Te Ture Whenua Māori land reform** | 2016–17 | **Not passed**; withdrawn by Labour in 2017 |
| Recognition of the NZ Wars (day of commemoration from 2017) | 2016–17 | Fox credited Flavell with this, and with work towards the pardon of Rua Kenana |

**What it cost.** The party gave confidence and supply to a government that:
- raised GST to 15% (2010);
- sold minority stakes in state power companies (67.3% opposed the sales in the 2013 citizens-initiated
  referendum);
- refused to entrench the Māori seats.

The party lost Harawira and the left of its base to Mana in 2011, and every election after 2008 brought a lower
vote. Labour's 2005 campaign line was that "a vote for the Māori Party is a vote for National". After nine years in
support of National, the party was wiped out in 2017.

## 4. Opposition, 2020–2026: protest politics

- **5 December 2023**: "National Māori Action Day" protests at the opening of Parliament. The party's MPs modify
  their oaths to refer to Te Tiriti.
- **December 2023**: Maipi-Clarke's maiden speech, which attracted wide attention. She said the new government had
  "attacked my whole world from every corner".
- **30 May 2024**: "Toitū Te Tiriti" national day of action on Budget day. The party calls for a Māori parliament.
- **14 November 2024**: at the first reading of ACT's **Treaty Principles Bill**, Maipi-Clarke tears up the bill and
  leads a haka, joined by both co-leaders and Labour's Peeni Henare. The Hīkoi mō te Tiriti reaches Parliament later
  that month ([background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C4%ABkoi_m%C5%8D_te_Tiriti)).
- **May–June 2025**: the Privileges Committee finds Maipi-Clarke, Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer in contempt for
  "acting in a manner that could have the effect of intimidating a member". It recommends suspensions of **7 days**
  (Maipi-Clarke) and **21 days** (each co-leader), the harshest it has ever proposed. The MPs had boycotted the
  hearing, calling it a "kangaroo court". Parliament imposed the suspensions on **5 June 2025** on a party-line vote.
  Labour agreed the rules were broken but proposed 24 hours.
- **February 2025**: Tākuta Ferris is found to have deliberately misled the House and told to apologise, after
  calling other MPs liars.
- **6 September 2025**: **Tāmaki Makaurau by-election**, after Kemp's death on 26 June 2025. **Oriini Kaipara** wins
  with 6,948 votes to Henare's 3,429. National, ACT, NZ First and the Greens did not stand.
- **October 2025**: Ferris and Ngarewa-Packer film themselves burning a copy of the new takutai moana amendment on
  Parliament's grounds.
- **September 2026**: Ngarewa-Packer is ordered out of the House for using an obscenity in an exchange with the
  Assistant Speaker.

## 5. Governance, finance and data controversies

- **2020 donations.** In April 2021 the Electoral Commission referred the party to Police for not disclosing about
  $320,000 of donations in time. These included $158,224 from Tamihere and $48,880 from the National Urban Māori
  Authority (NUMA). Police referred the case to the SFO, which **closed it in 2022 without prosecution**.
- **Charities and campaigns (2022).** Charities Services examined a $385,307 loan from the Te Whānau o Waipareira
  Trust group and $82,695 from NUMA towards Tamihere's 2020 campaign. Tamihere leads both organisations, and charities
  may not fund parties. Tamihere called the inquiry discrimination and the party boycotted the NZ Herald over its
  coverage.
- **Census and vaccination data (2023 election).** In 2024 former Manurewa Marae staff alleged that 2023 Census forms
  had been copied and the data used to target voters, and that people were given vouchers to switch to the Māori roll.
  Labour separately complained that texts from a Waipareira-registered short code urged people to vote for the party.
  The party denied wrongdoing. The PM ordered a Public Service Commission inquiry. Outcomes so far:
  - Stats NZ cleared the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency (January 2025);
  - Police and the SFO **stopped their criminal inquiry for lack of evidence** (October 2025);
  - privacy inquiries were continuing at last report.
  Rawiri Taonui and Radio Waatea disputed the allegations and linked the whistleblowers to Destiny Church.
- **Whānau Ora money and electioneering (2025).** Te Puni Kōkiri reviewed whether the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency
  (Te Pou Matakana) had misused funding on a campaign urging Māori to join the Māori roll. The agency had already lost
  its contract in a 2025 re-tender.
- **2023 policy apology.** The party apologised to migrant and refugee communities for "harmful narratives" on its
  website. These included an "Indigenous first" housing plank that would have curbed immigration. It also deleted a
  2020 sports-policy claim that "Māori genetic makeup is stronger than others"; Waititi denied the claim was racist.

## 6. The 2025–26 internal crisis

- **July 2025**: according to Tamihere, MPs Mariameno Kapa-Kingi (Te Tai Tokerau) and Tākuta Ferris (Te Tai Tonga)
  plotted to replace the co-leaders.
- **September 2025**: Ferris posts criticism of non-Māori Labour volunteers during the by-election. The party
  apologises for the post but Ferris refuses to. Kapa-Kingi is removed as whip.
- **October 2025**: Toitū Te Tiriti, led by Kapa-Kingi's son Eru, cuts ties with the party, alleging bullying and
  authoritarian leadership. A party email to members accuses Kapa-Kingi of a $133,000 office overspend and unpaid
  staff, and Eru of abusing a security guard. Founding member Amokura Panoho calls for Tamihere to resign. The
  co-leaders announce a "reset".
- **3 November 2025**: Tamihere publicly accuses the two MPs of "greed, avarice, and entitlement" and tells them to
  quit. The National Iwi Chairs Forum tries to mediate.
- **9 November 2025**: the national council **expels Kapa-Kingi and Ferris**. Former co-leader Flavell and a law
  expert question the process. Hone Harawira calls for reinstatement.
- **5 December 2025**: the High Court gives Kapa-Kingi interim reinstatement. On **10 March 2026** Justice Radich rules
  that her suspension and expulsion **breached the party's own rules and were unlawful**. The party says it will
  comply.
- **2026**: the Te Tai Tokerau and Te Tai Tonga electorate committees resign in support of the two MPs. Ferris
  will stand as an **independent** in Te Tai Tonga (from March 2026). Kapa-Kingi leaves and forms the **Te Tai Tokerau
  Party** (May 2026; registered August 2026). At Waitangi in February 2026 a confrontation between Eru Kapa-Kingi and
  party supporters ended any hope of reconciliation.

The crisis matters for voters because it splits the vote in two Māori seats, and because it raises questions about
how the party is run, given that it campaigns on mana motuhake and tikanga.

## 7. Election results, 2005–2023

| Election | Party votes | % | Seats | Electorates | Overhang | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2005 | — | 2.12 | 4 | 4 | 1 | Opposition |
| 2008 | 55,980 | 2.39 | 5 | 5 | 2 | Confidence & supply to National |
| 2011 | 31,982 | 1.43 | 3 | 3 | 1 | Confidence & supply to National |
| 2014 | 31,850 | 1.32 | 2 | 1 (Waiariki) | 0 | Confidence & supply to National |

(Te Tai Tonga). The **party list has one name**, secretary Lance Norman.

## 9. 2026 polling

Te Pāti Māori is polling **0.4%–2.2%** in party-vote surveys from August to October 2026. Examples: 1News–Verian 0.7%
(15–19 October); Freshwater Strategy 2.0% (9–19 October); RNZ–Reid Research 2.0%. That is below its 2023 result, but
it is also what the party's own strategy aims for: Te Pāti Māori is asking supporters to give their party vote to
Labour or the Greens. Its seat count depends on the Māori electorates, which are not covered by national polls. If it
wins more electorates than its party vote entitles it to, an **overhang** follows, as in 2023. Full series:
[`data/polls-2026.json`](../../data/polls-2026.json).

## 10. 2026 pitch and headline policies

The campaign was launched in Gisborne on 16 August 2026. It is built on getting Māori onto the Māori roll and on
strategic voting to remove the coalition. Headline commitments:

- **Constitution and Te Tiriti**:
  - an independent **Te Tiriti Commission** to investigate Crown breaches;
  - **binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations**;
  - a 2040 target for constitutional reform and a $200m **Mātike Mai** fund;
  - implement UNDRIP;
  - state accountability for te reo Māori.

  In February 2025 the party had demanded a Te Tiriti commissioner with veto power as a coalition "bottom line".
- **Justice**: **abolish prisons by 2040** and move to restorative justice.
- **Tax ("Kiwi Tax Plan")**:
  - first $30,000 tax-free (a rebate) and no GST on kai;
  - 48% top rate above $300,000;
  - a wealth tax starting at 1.5%;
  - a higher company tax rate and a 5% tax on profits sent offshore;
  - land-banking and vacant-home taxes, and a 5% stamp duty on residential sales.
- **Economy and kai**: Crown land and $100m for Māori supermarket collectives; support for the Māori economy.
- **Energy**: a $1b energy-sovereignty fund for Māori and community-owned renewables.
- **Environment**: ban seabed mining; assert tino rangatiratanga over freshwater.
- **Social services**:
  - a Māori Education Authority;
  - whānau-led care for Māori children;
  - Māori-led disability services;
  - a $200m Takatāpui Commission.
- **Foreign policy**: declare New Zealand "military neutral"; focus on the Pacific.

The full list is in [./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md).

## 11. Coalition stance

The party ruled out a right-wing coalition in 2022 and has kept to that. In 2026 it is campaigning openly for a
Labour–Green–Te Pāti Māori change of government. Labour, its main rival in the Māori seats, has rejected several key
policies:
- Hipkins ruled out a Te Tiriti commissioner able to overturn laws (February 2025);
- Labour is "dead-set against" abolishing prisons;
- Labour has ruled out the Te Tiriti Commission and Mātike Mai (September 2026).

Reactions to the constitutional package when it was announced (1 September 2026): Green co-leader Marama Davidson said it
aligned with "what we've had out there for years"; ACT leader David Seymour called the proposal "fundamentally
undemocratic" and said "you can't take these guys seriously"; NZ First deputy leader Shane Jones called it
"backward-looking", an "unnecessary burden on the economy", and said "I fear that it will further politicise the Treaty";
National's Paul Goldsmith said he disagreed with the reforms and that National upheld "the foundations of our democracy"
([RNZ, 1 Sep 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1207353/te-pati-maori-vows-major-constitutional-reform-by-making-te-tiriti-binding-for-crown);
[Te Ao Māori News, 2 Sep 2026](https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/09/02/te-pati-maoris-te-tiriti-entrenchment-plan-how-would-it-work-and-could-it-happen/)).

## Background

Kapa-Kingi won Te Tai Tokerau for [Te Pāti Māori](../te-pati-maori/README.md) in 2023 (by 517 votes over Labour's Kelvin
Davis). After tensions with the party leadership she was suspended in October 2025 and then expelled by its National
Council. policy.nz records that the suspension followed "accusations of mismanaging funds". On 10 March 2026 the High
Court (Justice Paul Radich) ruled the suspension and expulsion unlawful because the process did not follow the party's
kawa and tikanga as its constitution required. Te Pāti Māori accepted the ruling, but in May 2026 Stuff reported that the
two were not working together. [1][2][3]

## Foundation and 2026 campaign

- On 11 May 2026 Kapa-Kingi announced the new party, saying she would return to Te Pāti Māori only if president John
  Tamihere stood down, Te Tai Tonga MP Tākuta Ferris was returned to the party and the leadership apologised publicly.
  The split was widely reported as a break from Te Pāti Māori, which said it would contest all seven Māori seats
  (Aperahama Edwards is its Te Tai Tokerau candidate). [1][4]
- Labour's Chris Hipkins and National's Chris Bishop suggested the electorate-based name might breach electoral law; the
  Electoral Commission registered it on 5 August 2026, judging confusion not likely enough to refuse. [1][5]
- **Candidates:** list 1 **Kyla Campbell-Kamariera** (list only; former Te Pāti Māori Te Tai Tokerau electorate
  co-chair, previously no. 23 on TPM's list), list 2 **Mariameno Kapa-Kingi** (Te Tai Tokerau). Kapa-Kingi is seeking
  both votes; a big enough party vote could elect both. [1][6]
- She said she would consider working with National if Christopher Luxon sought her support, and would not rule out
  working with any party. [1]
- Donations: $50,000 from Richard Allen via the Stanley Howard Fund. [7]
- People: [Mariameno Kapa-Kingi](people/mariameno-kapa-kingi/). Policies: [policies/README.md](policies/README.md).

## History

United Future was formed for the 2002 election by merging Peter Dunne's liberal United New Zealand (founded by
moderate Labour and National MPs in 1995) with Future New Zealand, a "secularised" successor to the Christian
Democrats. Helped by a strong televised-debate performance by Dunne, it won 6.7% and eight seats in 2002, but fell to
2.7% and three seats in 2005 and, after its socially conservative wing (Gordon Copeland, Larry Baldock and others)
left over the 2007 "anti-smacking" law to form what became the Kiwi Party, to a single seat — Dunne's — from 2008.
Dunne then rebranded the party as a moderate centrist party. [1]

After 2005 Dunne gave confidence and supply to Helen Clark's Labour-led government and became Minister of Revenue
outside Cabinet. From 2008 to 2017 he supported John Key's and Bill English's National-led governments under three
written agreements (2008, 2011, 2014) — see the [track record](track-record.md). [1][2]

### The 2011–2017 period covered by this archive

- **2011:** United Future won 0.60% of the party vote. Dunne held Ōhāriu by 1,392 votes over Labour's Charles
  Chauvel, who called National's soft-pedalling in the seat an "unprincipled political deal". [1][3][4]
- **2013 deregistration episode:** On 31 May 2013 the Electoral Commission cancelled the party's registration at its
  own request because it could not show 500 financial members. The Speaker ruled Dunne would sit as an independent
  and lose party-leader funding until it re-registered; the Commission re-registered the party on 13 August 2013. [1][5][6]
- **GCSB-report leak (June 2013):** Dunne resigned his ministerial portfolios on 7 June 2013 after declining to give
  the Henry inquiry all his emails with a Fairfax journalist about the leak of the Kitteridge report on the GCSB. In
  December 2013 Parliament's Privileges Committee found he had been entitled to refuse, and he was reinstated as a
  minister on 28 January 2014. [7][8]
- **2014:** 0.22% of the party vote; Dunne held Ōhāriu by 710 votes over Labour's Ginny Andersen. [3][9]
- **2017:** On 21 August 2017, citing polling and a "mood for change" in Ōhāriu, Dunne announced his retirement.
  Damian Light became leader on 23 August. The party won 0.07% (1,782 votes) and lost its only seat; Labour's Greg
  O'Connor won Ōhāriu. [1][10]
- **Dissolution:** The party's AGM voted to disband in November 2017; Light and Dunne confirmed it on 14 November and
  the registration was cancelled on 28 February 2018. [1][11]

## Ideology and policy

Its 2007 mission statement described "a modern centre party" promoting "strong families and vibrant communities" and
"a competitive economy ... through market policies where possible, and government where necessary". Signature
policies in this period were **income splitting/sharing** for families, **flexible ("flexi") superannuation**, health
and medicines policy (Medicines New Zealand, a bigger role for pharmacists), recreational hunting/fishing interests
(a Game Animal Council) and, in 2011, limits on state-asset sales. [1][2]

## History

Vision NZ is the third party linked to the Tamakis' Destiny Church, after Destiny New Zealand (2003–07) and the Family
Party (2007–10). Its positions have included opposition to abortion and homosexuality, a call to ban construction of
new mosques, a (later qualified) two-year halt to immigration and refugees, removing non-citizen permanent residents'
right to vote — alongside support for a Māori-owned bank, Tūhoe ownership of Te Urewera and government funding for
Destiny Church programmes. Labour and National ruled out working with it by December 2019. [1]

In 2020 it ran a five-person list and won **0.15%**; Hannah Tamaki came third in Waiariki (1,171 votes). After Brian
Tamaki launched [Freedoms NZ](../freedoms-nz/README.md) in August 2022, Vision NZ became a component party; in 2023 it
contested all seven Māori electorates but the party vote went to Freedoms NZ (0.34%). Hannah Tamaki came last of five
in Tāmaki Makaurau (829 votes). In August–September 2023 Vision candidate Karl Mokaraka repeatedly disrupted Labour,
National and ACT campaign events. After Freedoms NZ deregistered (May 2025), Hannah Tamaki stood for Vision NZ in the
September 2025 Tāmaki Makaurau by-election (175 of 10,688 votes). [1][2]

A Vision member's High Court challenge to Wellington's Cuba Street rainbow crossing was dismissed in March 2025 with
costs awarded against the plaintiffs. [1]

# ACT New Zealand: track record, 2011–2026

This page covers promises against delivery, reliability, how ACT's actions in government lined up with its stated principles, and trends. Each entry, with its sources, is in [`data/promises/act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json). The party profile is in [README.md](./README.md) and 2026 policies are in [policies/README.md](./policies/README.md).

## How to read this

**Status definitions** (applied identically to every party in this archive):
- **kept**: delivered substantially as promised.
- **partially-kept**: some of it delivered, or delivered late or watered down.
- **broken**: not delivered, for whatever reason (ACT's own failure, a coalition partner's veto, or a lack of power).
- **abandoned**: ACT itself dropped or traded away the commitment, usually in coalition negotiations.
- **in-progress**: underway but not finished.
- **not-yet-due**: a 2026 promise.

**Context matters.** ACT had a single MP from 2011 to 2020 and was in opposition from 2017 to 2023. Being a junior partner limits what it can deliver. Many items below were *coalition-agreement* commitments, so they are a fair test of whether ACT secured and then delivered what it negotiated. Others were *campaign* promises that ACT traded away. The sample covers ACT's headline promises; it is not every manifesto line.

## Reliability scorecard

<!-- GENERATED:scorecard START -->
| Promises made at | kept | partially-kept | broken | abandoned | in-progress | not-yet-due | Total | Reliability* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 election/term | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 50% |
| 2014 election/term | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3 | 67% |
| 2017 election/term | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 100% |
| 2020 election/term | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 3 | 0% |
| 2023 election/term | 13 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 23 | 65% |
| long-standing | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 100% |
| 2026 (upcoming) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 5 | 5 | – |
| **All** | **18** | **4** | **5** | **6** | **0** | **5** | **38** | **61%** |

\*Reliability = (kept + ½ × partially-kept) ÷ (kept + partially-kept + broken + abandoned). In-progress and not-yet-due items are excluded. This is a rough indicator over a curated sample of headline promises, not a full audit of every manifesto line.
<!-- GENERATED:scorecard END -->

(This table is generated by `tools/record_act_nzf_scorecard.py` from the JSON.)

**Summary.**
- Of the commitments ACT secured in the **2023 coalition agreement**, most were delivered, and quickly: the Ministry for Regulation, the Regulatory Standards Act, charter schools, three strikes, interest deductibility, the Arms Act rewrite, 90-day trials, the Reserve Bank mandate, repeal of s7AA, and the Deputy PM rotation. The clear coalition failures were the 2017-size public service and the live-export reversal.
- ACT's biggest **campaign** promises fared worse when they met coalition partners. The Treaty-principles referendum was dropped in negotiations, and the Treaty Principles Bill was killed by National and NZ First. ACT's tax plan gave way to National's, and the abolition of demographic ministries, repeal of the Zero Carbon Act and abolition of the Māori seats were left out of the deal.
- In short, ACT is **highly reliable at delivering what it negotiates**, but negotiated away a good part of what it campaigned on.

## Promises vs delivery, by election

### 2011 (1 MP, John Banks; confidence and supply with National)
| Promise | Verdict | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Charter (partnership) schools | ✅ kept | Legislated; first five schools opened February 2014 |
| Near-flat ~15% income tax | ⛔ abandoned | Never enacted; ACT had dropped the flat tax by 2021 |
| Regulatory responsibility law | ✅ (eventually) | The 2011 bill failed; delivered in 2025 as the Regulatory Standards Act |

### 2014 (1 MP, David Seymour; confidence and supply)
| Promise | Verdict | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Expand charter schools (Seymour as Under-Secretary) | ✅ kept | More schools opened 2014–17 (17 approved); abolished by Labour in 2018 |
| Three strikes for burglary | ❌ broken | Never enacted; re-promised for 2026 |
| Replace the RMA | ✅ kept (2026) | Planning Act 2026 and Natural Environment Act 2026 passed in September 2026, after a long cross-government saga |

### 2017 (1 MP; opposition)
| Promise | Verdict | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Legalise assisted dying | ✅ kept | End of Life Choice Act passed 2019; approved at the 2020 referendum; in force November 2021. NZ First's referendum condition was the price of passage |

### 2020 (10 MPs; opposition)
| Promise | Verdict | What happened |

| Cut the middle tax rate (30% → 17.5%) | ❌ broken | In opposition; in 2023 National's package was adopted instead |
| Abolish Ministry for Women, Pacific Peoples, Ethnic Communities | ⛔ abandoned | Not in the 2023 deal; ministries remain; re-promised for 2026 |
| Abolish Māori seats; cut Parliament to 100 MPs | ⛔ abandoned | Not in the 2023 deal |

### 2023 ("Real Change"; 11 MPs; coalition)

|---|---|---|

| **Treaty Principles Act** | ❌ broken | First reading 68–54 (14 Nov 2024); ~300,000 submissions, ~90% opposed; defeated 112–11 at second reading (10 Apr 2025) |
| Ministry and Minister for Regulation | ✅ kept | Established 1 March 2024 |
| Regulatory Standards Act | ✅ kept | Passed 13 Nov 2025; in force 1 Jan 2026 |
| Charter schools return | ✅ kept | Law passed Sept 2024; 18 open by July 2026 (funding was for 50) |
| Interest deductibility restored faster | ✅ kept | 80% in 2024, 100% in 2025 |
| Pet bonds / tenancy reform | ✅ kept | Passed December 2024 |
| Three strikes reinstated | ✅ kept | Passed 13 Dec 2024; in force 17 June 2025 |
| Gang patch ban (National-led) | ✅ kept | September 2024 |
| Arms Act rewrite | ✅ kept | Arms Act 2026 (third reading 29 July 2026) |

| ACT's flatter tax cuts | ◑ partial | National's ~$14b package was enacted instead |
| 90-day trials; repeal Fair Pay Agreements; Reserve Bank single mandate | ✅ kept | December 2023 |
| Reverse live-export ban | ❌ broken | Cabinet would not agree (March 2026) |
| Repeal Zero Carbon Act; abolish Climate Change Commission | ⛔ abandoned | Not in the deal; re-promised for 2026 |
| Services based on need, not race | ◑ partial | Cabinet directive Sept 2024; Te Aka Whai Ora abolished; ACC targets dropped |
| Repeal s7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act | ✅ kept | April 2025, despite a Waitangi Tribunal finding |
| Cheaper school lunches | ✅ kept | ~$130m a year saved; quality complaints |
| Pharmac reform | ◑ partial | Seymour's July 2024 letter of expectations; $604m more medicines funding (Budget 2024); no structural model change |
| Four-year term | ⛔ abandoned | First reading March 2025, then shelved (February 2026) |
| Deputy PM rotation | ✅ kept | Seymour became Deputy PM on 31 May 2025 |

### 2026 (upcoming)
Headline promises are listed as *not-yet-due* in the JSON: a gradual rise in the NZ Super age, a three-year minimum wage freeze, disestablishing the Waitangi Tribunal after settlements, immigration restrictions, and "equal rights" entrenchment. See [policies/README.md](./policies/README.md).

## Alignment: did ACT's actions match its stated principles?

ACT's stated values are individual freedom, personal responsibility, "smaller, smarter government", equality before the law regardless of race, and freedom of expression "without restriction other than for incitement, criminal nuisance or defamation" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand)).

**Strongly consistent:**
- **Regulation and law-making quality.** ACT pursued this from Hide's 2006 bill through to the 2025 Act, and set up a dedicated ministry. It is the clearest example of a long-held policy turned into law.
- **"One law for all" / equal treatment.** ACT carried the Treaty Principles Bill to a vote despite record opposition, pushed the "need not race" directive, repealed s7AA, and removed ACC's ethnic targets. ACT presents these as applying its stated policy; critics, including the Waitangi Tribunal and Te Pāti Māori, see a breach of Treaty obligations. Either way, the actions match the stated policy.
- **Liberty-based dissent inside the coalition.** ACT voted against or withheld support from measures it saw as intrusive or protectionist: the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill (agree to disagree), the under-16 social media ban (2025 and 2026), the modern slavery bill, and gift-card expiry rules. It also opposed forced break-ups of supermarkets and power companies.
- **Earlier record.** Seymour was the lone vote against the 2019 firearms ban and campaigned on the Arms Act rewrite he later helped deliver. He also championed End of Life Choice.

**Tensions:**
- **Small government vs outcome.** ACT promised to return the public service to its 2017 size. Thousands of roles were cut, but full-time-equivalent numbers in June 2026 (63,912) were about where they were in June 2023, and far above 2017. ACT ministers were part of the government that set the spending path. ACT's 2026 fiscal plan in effect concedes this by re-promising 2017 spending levels.
- **Free expression vs gang patch ban.** ACT's principles allow only narrow limits on expression, yet it voted for the 2024 gang patch ban, a National policy.
- **Good law-making vs urgency.** ACT champions careful, principled law-making through the Regulatory Standards Act. Yet the government passed the 2025 pay-equity changes, led by ACT's van Velden, under urgency, without a select-committee stage ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Amendment_Act_2025)).
- **Immigration.** ACT's 2023 agreement leaned towards liberalising (for example a higher RSE cap and easier family visas). Its 2026 platform has turned restrictive, with benefit stand-downs, a work-visa surcharge and abolition of the permanent-resident category.
- **The referendum "condition".** In 2022 ACT said a Treaty referendum would be a condition of coalition. It dropped that condition in 2023, which shows the gap between campaign framing and negotiating reality.

## Trends (2011 → 2026)

1. **From vehicle to force.** ACT went from 1.07% (2011), 0.69% (2014) and 0.50% (2017), surviving only through the Epsom arrangement, to 7.58% (2020) and 8.64% (2023). It polls about 6–11% in 2026. Its influence shifted from a single member's bill to three Cabinet ministers and a Deputy PM.
2. **Delivery improved with seats.** With one MP, ACT's main win was a conscience-vote member's bill (End of Life Choice) and a few concessions in support agreements (charter schools). With 11 MPs it secured and largely delivered about 20 coalition commitments within three years. Several of them (charter schools, the Regulatory Standards Act, three strikes) revived policies that a previous government had reversed.
3. **Reversals.** ACT's signature policies have been reversed by Labour before: charter schools in 2018 and three strikes in 2022. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the 2024–25 versions, so their future depends on the 2026 result.
4. **Consistent priorities.** Smaller government, deregulation, longer sentences, firearms-owner rights and "equal citizenship" run through every campaign since 2014. The Treaty and co-governance became the dominant theme from 2022.
5. **Party organisation.** ACT has gained donors and staff: it overtook Labour in 2025 donations, held a 2024 campaign-culture review, entered local government (ACT Local, 2025), and changed its deputy (McKee replaced van Velden in 2026).

# Green Party: track record, 2008–2026

> How reliable have the Greens been? What did they promise, what did they deliver in government, where did they
> compromise, and do their actions match their values? Current to 23 October 2026.
> Data: [`data/promises/green.json`](../../data/promises/green.json) (32 entries) · Profile: [README](./README.md) ·
> 2026 policies: [./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md)

## How to read this

- **kept**: delivered substantially as promised. **partially-kept**: delivered in a smaller or later form.
  **broken**: not delivered, or the party acted against the commitment. **abandoned**: the party dropped or
  scaled back the commitment. **not-yet-due**: a 2026 pledge.
- "Broken" here means **not delivered**, whatever the reason. Each entry's `detail` says whether the Greens
  actually had the power to deliver. Greens have only ever been a **support partner**. They never held a Cabinet
  seat or a majority, so most of their wins depended on Labour agreeing. Where a Green-backed measure was carried by a
  Labour minister, we say so.
- The tracker is a sample of the most significant, verifiable commitments. It is not every manifesto line.

## 1. Scorecard

Counts from `green.json` (32 entries):

| Status | Count | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| kept | 11 | Zero Carbon Act; cannabis referendum; Healthy Homes; Mental Health Commission; oil & gas exploration ban; refugee quota doubled; Clean Car Discount; 2030 target raised to 50%; Samoan citizenship bill |
| partially-kept | 4 | Welfare increases (smaller than promised); renters' rights (no rent cap); Green Transport Card (only in 2023); medicinal cannabis (via the government's bill) |
| broken | 6 | Agricultural emissions pricing; Auckland light rail; wealth tax (2020); waka-jumping principle; no state money for private schools (Green School); right-to-repair bill |
| abandoned | 1 | 2023 wealth-tax and Guaranteed Minimum Income design (scaled back for 2026) |
| not-yet-due | 10 | 2026 tax plan, rent cap, KiwiMart, Kiwipower, school lunches, pay equity, rail, donations cap, union membership, Fast-track repeal |

Of the 22 commitments that can be assessed, **15 (68%) were kept or partially kept**. Most of these date from
2017–20, when the Greens had a written agreement and Labour needed their votes. Two of the six "broken" items were
cases where the Greens acted against their own stated principles (waka-jumping, Green School). The other four were
outcomes they could not force.

## 2. Term by term

### 2008–2011: opposition, with a policy MoU with National
- After the 2008 election the Greens signed a memorandum of understanding with John Key's National government
  (April 2009). It covered policy cooperation, not confidence and supply, and lapsed in 2011
  ([Fifth National Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand)). This is the
  only formal Green arrangement with National. We could not retrieve the MoU text in this pass: the Beehive PDF
  link returns 404.
- **Assessment:** shows the Greens could work across the aisle on specific issues while keeping their independence.

### 2011–2014: opposition
- The Greens' strongest opposition term, with 11.06% and 14 MPs. Russel Norman named his main wins as forcing the
  government to reverse its plan to open Schedule 4 conservation land to mining, and leading the campaign for the
  citizens-initiated referendum on asset sales. 67.3% voted against the sell-downs, but the referendum was not binding
  and the sales went ahead
  ([RNZ profile](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/264907/profile-russel-norman);
  [Fifth National Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand)).

### 2014–2017: opposition; the Turei crisis
- Labour and the Greens went into the 2017 election under a memorandum of understanding to campaign together. NZ First later used this as a reason not to negotiate directly with the Greens ([Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11931588)).
- In July 2017 Metiria Turei disclosed past benefit fraud to make the case for welfare reform. Support briefly rose to
  15%. Then two MPs quit the caucus and on 9 August 2017 she resigned, and the vote fell to 6.27%. This is the clearest
  example of a "values" campaign that went wrong electorally
  ([Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11901089);
  [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/95549623/greens-in-crisis-metiria-turei-stays-on-despite-mps-quitting)).

### 2017–2020: confidence & supply, three ministers outside Cabinet
**Delivered**
- **Zero Carbon Act (2019)**: net-zero 2050 target, Climate Change Commission and five-yearly emissions budgets.
  Passed with almost unanimous support; National backed it from the first reading. Biogenic methane was given a
  separate target (24–47% below 2017 by 2050) rather than net zero.
- **Cannabis referendum** held in 2020; it narrowly failed, with 50.7% voting no.
- **Medicinal cannabis** legalised (December 2018) through the government's bill. The Green member's bill had been
  voted down.
- **End to new offshore oil and gas exploration** (April 2018).
- **Healthy Homes Guarantee Act 2017**; **Mental Health Commission** re-established (Te Hiringa Mahara).
- **Refugee quota** raised to 1,500 from 2020, the Greens' "double the quota" pledge.
- **Renters' rights** (2020): rent rises limited to once a year, no-cause evictions ended, rental bidding banned. No
  rent cap.
- **Benefits**: up $25 a week from April 2020. The bigger increases came in 2021–22.

**Not delivered or compromised**
- **Light rail to Auckland Airport**: not started by 2020, and still not built when Labour left office.
- **Waka-jumping law**: the Greens voted for it in 2018 against their long-held position, because of their duty to
  let the Labour–NZ First deal be implemented. A spokesperson said negotiators "forgot" to register their opposition.
  Shaw called it the party's "most difficult decision". In July 2020 they voted to repeal it, and Peters called them
  "untrustworthy".
- **Green School grant** (August 2020): $11.7m for a private school, against Green policy. Shaw apologised for an
  "error of judgment" and the grant became a loan.
- **Iraq and Afghanistan deployments**: the Greens had been the most consistent critics in Parliament, but did little
  in government to oppose extensions (Hansard). Peters played down Green claims that the 2019 Iraq withdrawal was
  their win ([Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/winston-peters-a-bit-hard-to-argue-decision-to-bring-kiwi-troops-home-was-a-green-win/WHWKCWTU2CI5CJIN3QWPCIEPZY/)).

### 2020–2023: cooperation agreement, two ministers outside Cabinet, Labour majority
**Delivered or advanced (under Green ministers or with Green support)**
- **2030 Paris target raised** from a 30% to a 50% cut in net emissions (October 2021, Shaw).
- **Clean Car Discount** (July 2021 to December 2023). EVs rose to about 27% of new car sales by the end of 2023.
- **Benefits indexed to wages** and lifted by $32–55 a week (Budget 2021). RNZ reported this reversed the 1991 cuts in
  real terms.
- **Drug checking** made permanently legal (2021), a world first, through a government bill.
- **Discounted public transport** for Community Services Card holders made permanent from July 2023. This is a late,
  partial version of the 2017 "Green Transport Card".

**Not delivered**
- **Wealth tax**: ruled out by Ardern during the campaign. A majority Labour government did not need Green votes.
- **Agricultural emissions pricing** (pledged for 2025): not implemented before Labour lost office. The coalition
  dropped it in June 2024.
- **Light rail**: about $228m spent with no track laid. Cancelled in November 2023.
- **The 2023 "policy bonfire"**: Hipkins dropped or delayed several measures the Greens wanted, including hate-speech
  law and lowering the voting age to 16
  ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483875/watch-tvnz-rnz-merger-scrapped-income-insurance-and-hate-speech-laws-delayed);
  [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/03/13/pms-policy-bonfire-voting-age-bill-transport-schemes-reprioritsed/)).

**Internal cost.** Members and former MPs (Norman, Bradford, Delahunty) said the agreement gave the party too little
leverage. Shaw survived two leadership challenges, in 2021 and 2022
([RNZ, Jan 2022](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/459250/green-party-discontent-members-walk-ex-mps-criticise-leadership)).

### 2023–2026: opposition
- **Legislation passed from opposition:** Teanau Tuiono's bill restoring citizenship to Samoans born 1924–49 passed
  unanimously (November 2024).
- **Member's bills that failed:** Shaw's environmental Bill of Rights bill (defeated at first reading, April 2024).
  Davidson's right-to-repair bill passed its first reading but stalled after NZ First withdrew support.
- **Reversals of Green-era gains** by the National-led government, all opposed by the Greens:
  - Clean Car Discount repealed (December 2023);
  - Auckland light rail cancelled;
  - agriculture kept out of the ETS;
  - methane target lowered (October 2025);
  - 90-day no-cause evictions restored (December 2024);
  - Te Aka Whai Ora abolished (February 2024).

  Much of what the Greens won in 2017–23 has proved easy to reverse.
- **Votes:** consistent opposition to the coalition's Treaty Principles Bill, Fast-track Approvals Act, Māori wards
  referendums, three strikes and the Electoral Amendment Act 2025 (enrolment cut-off, prisoner voting ban). One
  notable cross-party vote: the Greens voted for the coalition's online casino bill at its first reading in July 2025
  ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/566995/online-casino-bill-greens-vote-with-coalition-govt-to-pass-first-reading)).
  We did not find their stated reasons in this pass.
- **Conduct:** more MPs lost or disciplined this term than any other party. See §5 and the [profile](./README.md#6-caucus-departures-and-discipline-20232026).

## 3. Reliability by term (qualitative)

| Term | Role | Leverage | Delivery against promises | Keeping to stated principles | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2008–11 | Opposition (MoU with National) | Low | n/a | High | Cross-party work without giving confidence and supply |
| 2011–14 | Opposition | Low | n/a (asset-sales referendum won, sales went ahead) | High | Peak campaigning strength |
| 2014–17 | Opposition | Low | n/a | Mixed | Turei's admission was a deliberate values campaign; caucus split |
| 2017–20 | Confidence & supply | **High** (Labour needed their votes) | **Good**: most headline items delivered (Zero Carbon, referendum, Healthy Homes, quota) | **Mixed**: waka-jumping vote, Green School grant | Best term for delivery |
| 2020–23 | Cooperation agreement | Low (Labour majority) | **Moderate**: climate target, Clean Car Discount, benefit rises; no wealth tax, no farm pricing, no light rail | Mostly consistent | Members questioned the value of the deal |
| 2023–26 | Opposition | None | One member's bill passed | Accountable but turbulent: Tana expelled, Genter censured, Ghahraman resigned | Record polling despite scandals |

## 4. Did they stick to their word?

- **On coalition partners: yes.** The Greens have only ever backed Labour-led governments. They have said so before
  each election and kept to it.
- **On their core agenda: largely yes, when they had leverage.** The 2017 agreement was mostly honoured. Zero Carbon,
  the referendum, Healthy Homes and the Mental Health Commission were all delivered.
- **On process principles: not always.** The 2018 waka-jumping vote and the 2020 Green School grant broke stated Green
  positions to keep the government arrangement working or to win a local project. In 2024 the party used the
  waka-jumping law itself to remove Tana, a law it had joined National in trying to repeal in 2020
  ([Te Ao Māori News, 17 Oct 2024](https://teaonews.co.nz/2024/10/17/greens-unanimously-vote-to-remove-darleen-tana-from-parliament)).
  Three senior Pasifika members resigned in protest (see the [profile, §6](./README.md#6-caucus-departures-and-discipline-20232026)).
- **On economic promises: scaled back over time, then pushed forward again.** The 2020 wealth tax and the 2023
  Guaranteed Minimum Income were never achieved. The 2026 tax plan is noticeably more modest: the wealth tax
  threshold rose from $2m to $10m. The 2026 platform adds new state intervention in markets: KiwiMart, rent caps and
  Kiwipower.

## 5. Actions vs values

| Value or position | Action | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Grassroots democracy; MPs' freedom of conscience | Voted for the waka-jumping law in 2018 under the support agreement; voted to repeal it in 2020–21; used it against Tana in 2024 | Inconsistent: the party voted for the law in 2018, tried to repeal it in 2020–21, then used it in 2024, giving reasons at each step. Fitzsimons opposed the 2018 vote. |
| Public education (no state money for private schools) | $11.7m Green School grant (2020) | Breach. The party admitted it and the grant became a loan. |
| Non-violence and peace | Muted on troop extensions in government (2017–20); in 2026, ex-NZSAS candidate Josh Jacobsen ranked 25 | Mixed. Critics have questioned the candidacy (a blog post, not independent reporting; see the README sources). |
| Social justice and workers' rights | Tana's role in the migrant-worker complaints at her husband's business (2024) | Breach by an individual MP. The party responded with an independent investigation, a call to resign, then expulsion. |
| Integrity and honesty | Ghahraman shoplifting convictions (2024) | Breach by an individual MP. She resigned within a week of the first report. |
| Safe, respectful workplaces | Bullying allegations against Kerekere (2023); Genter found in contempt (2024) | Breaches alleged or found. Kerekere said the process denied her natural justice, and Māori, Pasifika and Rainbow members defended her (see the profile, §6). |
| Te Tiriti partnership | 2022 rule that one co-leader must be Māori; Māori electorate candidates in 2026; consistent votes against the Treaty Principles Bill | Consistent. Pasifika and Māori members who resigned in 2024 alleged that Māori and Pasifika MPs were mistreated. |
| Palestinian self-determination | Consistent since 2021: motions, a sanctions bill, Swarbrick's 2025 suspension | Consistent. The New Zealand Jewish Council objected to Swarbrick's November 2023 "river to the sea" chant, a phrase RNZ noted many Israelis regard as antisemitic ([RNZ Morning Report, 7 Nov 2023](https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningreport/audio/2018914306/nz-jewish-council-on-swarbrick-s-comments-at-palestinian-rally)); she apologised to those offended but defended the phrase. |
| Climate | Zero Carbon Act; NDC raised; oil & gas ban; consistent opposition to rollbacks | Strongly consistent. The main gap was failing to get agricultural pricing in 2017–23. |

## 6. Trends

1. **Better at the ballot box in opposition than in government.** The vote fell from 10.7% to 6.3% at the 2017 crisis
   election, recovered only to 7.9% after the first government term, then jumped to 11.6% in opposition. 2026 polling
   is at a record 12–16%.
2. **Leverage drives delivery.** The 2017–20 term, when Labour needed Green votes, delivered far more than 2020–23,
   when it did not.
3. **Gains are easy to reverse.** Much of the 2017–23 legacy has been rolled back since 2023: Clean Car Discount,
   light rail, farm pricing, the methane target, tenancy rules. The Zero Carbon Act's framework has survived.
4. **The caucus has become less stable.** Five MPs from the 2023 caucus or their replacements left early:
   Ghahraman, Collins (died), Shaw, Tana and Doyle. Kerekere had quit in 2023. Three MPs this term faced conduct
   findings or criminal charges: Ghahraman, Tana and Genter.
5. **The platform has moved from "green growth" to economic populism.** Under Shaw the party courted business and
   fiscal credibility (the 2017 Budget Responsibility Rules). Under Swarbrick and Davidson it campaigns on wealth taxes,
   a state supermarket and public ownership, while dropping the most expensive 2023 designs.

# Labour Party — track record, promises and reliability (2011–2026)

[← Labour profile](./README.md) · [2026 policies](./policies/README.md) · Machine-readable tracker: [`data/promises/labour.json`](../../data/promises/labour.json) (92 entries, built by `tools/record_labour_build.py`)

*Compiled 23 October 2026. Verdicts are ours, applied with the same rules used for every party in this archive (see [Method](#10-method-and-caveats)). Every verdict links to independent sources — mainly RNZ, 1News, Newshub, Stuff, NZ Herald, The Spinoff, Newsroom, official documents (Treasury/IRD, MBIE, HUD, MSD, Kāinga Ora, Office of the Auditor-General, Royal Commission reports) and Wikipedia for legislative dates. Where sources disagree we say so.*

---

## Summary

**Labour's record over the last five elections splits sharply in two.**

1. **In opposition (2011, 2014)** Labour ran on a capital gains tax, raising the pension age to 67, NZ Power and KiwiAssure, lost twice, and **dropped every one of them** before 2017. The CGT has returned in 2026 in a narrower form.
2. **In government (2017–2023)** Labour delivered most of its *legislative and money-transfer* promises — the 100-day plan, Families Package, fees-free first year, minimum wage to $20, Healthy Homes, foreign-buyer ban, Zero Carbon Act, 10 sick days, Matariki, Fair Pay Agreements, 39% top tax rate. But it **failed on most of its big physical-delivery targets** — KiwiBuild's 100,000 homes, Auckland light rail (promised twice), the migration cut — and only partly met its child-poverty, mental-health, police and tree-planting targets.

| Scored promises (testable in office) | Number | Share |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ Kept | 36 | 59% |
| 🟡 Partially kept | 10 | 16% |
| ❌ Broken | 7 | 11% |
| ⛔ Abandoned by Labour | 8 | 13% |
| **Total** | **61** | |

Plus 7 opposition-era promises (2011/2014, all abandoned), 5 from the lost 2023 campaign, and 19 groups of 2026 promises (not yet due) — 92 entries in all.

**Key nuance:** coalition partner NZ First blocked or diluted several Labour policies in 2017–20 (CGT, water charges, three-strikes repeal, light rail, 90-day trials); COVID-19 dominated 2020–22. But the 2020–23 majority term — when Labour had no partner able to block it — produced its own broken promise on tax, a second light-rail failure, the mandatory Three Waters U-turn, and a 2023 "policy bonfire" of its own initiatives. Many of the promises it did keep were reversed by the 2023–26 coalition within months (see [Durability](#durability-what-survived-the-change-of-government)).

## 1. Opposition-era promises (2011 & 2014)

Labour lost both elections, so these could not be tested in office. They matter for **consistency**: did Labour keep campaigning on what it said it believed?

| Promise | Made | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capital gains tax (excluding family home) | 2011 (Goff), 2014 (Cunliffe) | Dropped by Andrew Little, confirmed at the 2015 conference; no CGT in Little's first-term plans. Ardern revived the idea via the Tax Working Group, then ruled it out (2019); Hipkins ruled it out again (2023), then adopted a narrower property CGT in October 2025. [ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/node/362358) · [interest.co.nz](https://www.interest.co.nz/news/54387/election-2011-party-policies-tax) · [interest.co.nz 2015](https://www.interest.co.nz/news/78527/labour-says-wont-introduce-capital-gains-tax-first-term-shelves-nz-power-plan-twyford) | ⛔ |
| Raise NZ Super age 65 → 67 | 2011, 2014 | Dropped by Little; "not while I'm leader" (2017). Age kept at 65 in government. [ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/node/362358) · [Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2017/03/labour-probably-won-t-raise-taxes-andrew-little.html) | ⛔ |
| GST off fresh fruit and vegetables | 2011 | Dropped under Cunliffe; revived in 2023. [ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/node/288951) | ⛔ |
| Compulsory KiwiSaver (employer contributions to 7%) | 2011 | Not carried forward; a version reappears in 2026. [interest.co.nz](https://www.interest.co.nz/news/54392/election-2011-party-policies-tax-kiwisaver) | ⛔ |
| NZ Power single electricity buyer (with Greens) | 2014 | Shelved by Little. [interest.co.nz](https://www.interest.co.nz/news/78527/labour-says-wont-introduce-capital-gains-tax-first-term-shelves-nz-power-plan-twyford) | ⛔ |
| KiwiAssure state insurer | 2014 | Reviewed in 2015, never revived. [interest.co.nz](https://www.interest.co.nz/news/73751/little-re-consider-labours-plan-establish-new-state-owned-insurer-kiwiassure) | ⛔ |
| 36% top tax rate | 2014 | Dropped; Labour later legislated 39% (2021). [ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/politics/labour-surplus-bid-relies-tax-rises) | ⛔ |

**Pattern:** after two defeats Labour concluded its "brave" policies were electoral liabilities. Little's reset — fewer, simpler, popular promises — set up the 2017 platform. Fair-minded reading: dropping policies voters rejected is normal democratic responsiveness; but the CGT's cycle (promised 2011/14 → dropped 2015 → revived 2017 → ruled out 2019 → ruled out 2023 → promised 2025/26) is the clearest example of Labour saying it believes in a policy while repeatedly declining to put it to voters or implement it.
