## 2. 2017 manifesto, 100-day plan and coalition agreements (2017–20 term)

Context: Labour won 36.9% and governed in **coalition with NZ First**, with **confidence & supply from the Greens**. Both agreements added commitments (NZ First: $1b/yr regional fund, 1,800 police, 1 billion trees, minimum wage path; Greens: Zero Carbon Act, cannabis referendum). NZ First also vetoed some Labour policies.

### 2a. The 100-day plan
| Promise | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 100-day plan (fees-free first year, student allowance +$50, Healthy Homes Bill, foreign-buyer ban, stop state-house sales, Families Package, child poverty bill, mental health inquiry, Tax Working Group, Pike River agency, cancel National's tax cuts, etc.) | Largely ticked off by February 2018, although several items were met by *introducing* a bill or *starting* an inquiry. [Newshub (plan)](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/election/2017/09/labour-announces-top-priorities-if-elected.html) · [1News halfway check](https://www.1news.co.nz/2017/12/12/halfway-point-in-governments-100-day-plan-sees-pm-pleased-with-progress/) · [Newstalk ZB](https://newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/govt-100-day-plan-whats-left-on-the-to-do-list) | ✅ |

### 2b. Housing
| Promise | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **KiwiBuild: 100,000 affordable homes in 10 years** | Interim targets missed by a wide margin (452 homes by June 2020 against an original 16,000 path); in the Sept 2019 "reset" Megan Woods scrapped the 100,000 target. **2,335** KiwiBuild homes completed July 2018 – Feb 2024 (+1,238 contracted). [Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/04-09-2019/cheat-sheet-megan-woods-hits-reset-on-the-beleaguered-kiwibuild-programme/) · [Newsroom](https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2019/09/04/789917/government-introduces-major-kiwibuild-overhaul) · [Kāinga Ora OIA](https://www.kaingaora.govt.nz/assets/Publications/OIAs-Official-Information-Requests/April-2024/9-April-2024-Breakdown-of-KiwiBuild-homes-by-Region-and-Price1.pdf) | ❌ |
| KiwiBuild: 1,000 homes in year one | Cut to 300 in Jan 2019; ~258 built by mid-2019, in what Ardern had called the "Year of Delivery". [Newsroom](https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2019/01/29/419945/kiwibuild-under-microscope-after-target-shortfall) · [Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2019/07/year-of-delivery-political-party-leaders-judge-the-government-s-progress.html) | ❌ |
| Stop state-house sales; build 1,000+ state houses a year | Sales stopped. Net public housing up ~10,000 Oct 2017–Jun 2022 (Labour: 13,000+ by 2023, "most since the 1950s"). Disputed: many "places" were purchases/leases, and a ~5,000-home pipeline was inherited from National. [Newshub explainer](https://newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/07/explainer-is-labour-fudging-state-house-numbers.html) · [AAP FactCheck](https://www.aap.com.au/factcheck/labour-and-national-both-claim-credit-for-nz-public-housing-rise/) | ✅ |
| Healthy Homes Guarantee Act | Passed Dec 2017; Labour itself later extended compliance deadlines to July 2025 (private) / 2024 (Kāinga Ora). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_Homes_Guarantee_Act_2017) · [HUD](https://www.hud.govt.nz/news/changes-to-the-healthy-homes-standards-compliance-timeframes) | ✅ |
| Ban foreign buyers of existing homes | Law passed Aug 2018 (Australians/Singaporeans exempt). Coalition added a $5m+ exemption for investor-visa holders in 2025. [NZ Law Society](https://www.lawsociety.org.nz/news/newsroom/ban-on-most-foreign-buyers-of-existing-homes-passed/) · [OneRoof](https://www.oneroof.co.nz/news/nzs-top-agents-surprised-as-foreign-buyer-ban-quietly-reversed-48757) | ✅ |

**Outcome context:** despite these measures, house prices rose sharply in the low-interest COVID period — the national median hit a record $925,000 in November 2021, up 23.8% in a year ([1News/REINZ](https://www.1news.co.nz/2021/12/12/median-house-price-in-nz-hits-record-high-in-november/)) — before falling ~17% as the Reserve Bank raised rates. Housing affordability, Labour's central 2017 theme, worsened during its first four years in office.

### 2c. Transport and infrastructure
| Promise | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Light rail CBD–Mt Roskill in 4 years, to the airport in 10** | Process lurched between NZTA, an unsolicited NZ Super Fund/CDPQ bid and light metro; NZ First blocked a decision in 2020. No track laid. ## 3. COVID-19 response

| Commitment | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Elimination strategy ("go hard, go early") | Achieved elimination through 2020–mid-2021; among the lowest COVID death rates in the developed world and negative excess mortality to early 2023 (Royal Commission phase 1). Elimination abandoned in October 2021 after Delta. Phase 2 (March 2026): "broadly effective but flawed" — criticism of lockdown duration, mandates' effect on social cohesion, overuse of urgency, and a slow exit. Ardern and Robertson: "We got a lot right. More than most." [1News (phase 1)](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/11/28/first-phase-of-royal-commission-of-inquiry-into-covid-19-released/) · [Spinoff (phase 2)](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/10-03-2026/covid-19-inquiry-makes-final-findings-on-spending-mandates-and-lockdowns) · [ODT/RNZ](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/national/covid-response-broadly-effective-some-flaws-inquiry-finds) | 🟡 |

**Cost-of-living aftermath.** Heavy pandemic spending, low interest rates and global shocks were followed by inflation of **7.3% in the year to June 2022**, a 32-year high ([1News/Stats NZ](https://1news.co.nz/2022/07/18/inflation-rises-to-73-a-32-year-high/)). The government responded with a temporary 25c fuel-excise cut, half-price public transport and a cost-of-living payment ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand)), and from 2023 Hipkins re-centred the government on "bread and butter" issues. Economists differ on how much of the inflation was domestic policy vs. global; we do not adjudicate that here.

## 6. Reliability scorecard

### By term (scored promises only)

| Term | Scored | ✅ Kept | 🟡 Partly | ❌ Broken | ⛔ Abandoned | Kept or partly |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2017–20 (coalition with NZ First; Green C&S) | 38 | 22 (58%) | 9 (24%) | 4 (11%) | 3 (8%) | 82% |
| 2020–23 (Labour majority) | 23 | 14 (61%) | 1 (4%) | 3 (13%) | 5 (22%) | 65% |
| **Total** | **61** | **36 (59%)** | **10 (16%)** | **7 (11%)** | **8 (13%)** | **75%** |

Of the 3 first-term abandonments, 2 (CGT, water royalty) were driven by NZ First; the third (fees-free years 2–3) was Labour's own choice. **All 5 second-term abandonments were Labour's own decisions**, made with a majority.

### By type of promise

| Type | Examples | Scored | Kept | Partly | Broken/abandoned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Big physical-delivery or numeric outcome targets** | KiwiBuild 100k and year-one, light rail ×2, migration cut, 1,800 police, 1bn trees, child poverty, mental health, rivers, Pike River, public housing ×2 | 13 | 2 | 6 | 5 |
| **Laws, regulations, transfers, taxes, inquiries** | 100-day plan, Families Package, min wage, Healthy Homes, foreign buyers, Zero Carbon, sick leave, Matariki, FPAs, 39% rate, abortion, conversion ban | 48 | 34 | 4 | 10 |

This is the single clearest finding: **when a promise could be delivered by passing a law, changing a payment or announcing a review, Labour usually delivered it (about 71% kept outright); when it required building things or hitting an outcome number, it kept 2 of 13 outright** — and the two it "kept" (public housing) are disputed on counting method.

### Durability: what survived the change of government
At least 15 kept promises were reversed or substantially wound back by the 2023–26 National–ACT–NZ First coalition, most within its first year: Fair Pay Agreements, smokefree generation, Three Waters, Te Aka Whai Ora, three-strikes repeal, Clean Car Discount, oil and gas ban, interest-deductibility removal, free prescriptions, youth public transport fares, fees-free first year (converted to final year), Te Pūkenga, light rail, the 2023/24 child-poverty targets (lowered) and the foreign-buyer ban (partial exemption) ([OAG](https://www.oag.parliament.nz/2025/child-poverty/part1.htm); other sources on each entry in the JSON). Several were rushed through late in the 2020–23 term or legislated without cross-party support, which made reversal easy. Measures with broader support (Zero Carbon Act, Healthy Homes standards, Matariki, conversion-practices ban, minimum wage path, 10 sick days, Families Package) have largely survived.

| **End child poverty / wellbeing** | Families Package, Best Start, benefit increases and wage indexation, free school lunches, free period products in schools, Child Poverty Reduction Act, wellbeing budgets ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand)) | Material hardship rose again in 2022/23; most targets for the second period missed |
| **Workers and unions** | Minimum wage raised from $15.75 to $20 (2017–21), FPAs, sick leave, pay equity settlements, 90-day trial limits | Social insurance scheme dropped |
| **Climate leadership ("nuclear-free moment")** | Zero Carbon Act, oil & gas ban, ETS reform, Clean Car standard, 2030 target raised to a 50% net cut ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand)) | Biofuel mandate and Clean Car Upgrade dropped in 2023 to ease costs; oil and gas ban was not in the 2017 manifesto |
| **Te Tiriti partnership** | Matariki holiday, Te Aka Whai Ora, Ihumātao purchase, iwi representation in water entities | Wikipedia's account of the 2023 election records criticism that the shared-governance changes (Three Waters entities, Te Aka Whai Ora) had not been clearly put to voters in 2020; in 2023 Labour lost five Māori seats to Te Pāti Māori, keeping only Ikaroa-Rāwhiti ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election)) |
| **Transparency / "be kind"** | Wellbeing reporting; Royal Commissions (abuse in care, COVID) | Heavy use of urgency (criticised by the COVID Royal Commission); mandatory Three Waters after saying it was optional; Ardern's silence on cannabis until after the vote; several ministerial resignations |

### Notable U-turns
1. **Capital gains tax** — promised 2011 and 2014; dropped 2015; reopened 2017; ruled out 2019 "while I'm leader"; ruled out 2023 "end of story"; promised again October 2025. ([timeline sources above](#1-opposition-era-promises-2011--2014))
2. **Tax timing, Sept 2017** — Ardern's mid-campaign switch from "could legislate a CGT this term" to "no changes until after 2020". ([Newsroom](https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2017/09/14/47849/labour-hits-pause-at-2359-on-doomsday-clock))
3. **Bright-line, March 2021** — ruled out in the 2020 campaign, enacted five months after the election. ([Newshub](https://newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/03/finance-minister-grant-robertson-admits-being-too-definitive-in-ruling-out-bright-line-extension-during-election.html))
4. **KiwiBuild target scrapped, Sept 2019.** ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/04-09-2019/cheat-sheet-megan-woods-hits-reset-on-the-beleaguered-kiwibuild-programme/))
5. **Fees-free three years dropped, Sept 2020.** ([Times Higher Education](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/cn/news/no-extension-new-zealands-fee-free-scheme))
6. **COVID elimination abandoned, Oct 2021** — defensible after Delta, but a reversal of the core strategy. ([Royal Commission via Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/10-03-2026/covid-19-inquiry-makes-final-findings-on-spending-mandates-and-lockdowns))
7. **Three Waters: optional → mandatory (2021) → four entities → ten (2023).** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Waters_reform_programme))
8. **Policy bonfire, 2023** (RNZ/TVNZ merger, income insurance, biofuels, hate speech, voting age 16).
9. **Interest deductibility** — Labour removed it (2021), opposed its restoration, then in September 2026 ruled out changing it again. ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/09/21/labour-rules-out-interest-deductibility-changes-for-landlords/))
10. **Three strikes** — repeal dropped in 2018 under NZ First pressure; done in 2022. (Delayed, not abandoned.)

---

## 8. Trends

- **Volatile support, personality-driven.** 27% (2011) → 25% (2014) → 37% (2017, after Ardern replaced Little) → 50% (2020, COVID rally) → 27% (2023) → ~27–31% in October 2026 polls after leading through early 2026 ([README](./README.md#2026-polling)).
- **Ambition outran delivery capacity.** Labour's signature 2017 promises were large build/outcome targets that depended on state delivery capability it did not have (KiwiBuild, light rail). Its later promises have become smaller, costed, and transfer- or regulation-based (fare caps, free GP visits, KiwiSaver settings) — a lesson visibly learned, though the 2026 NZ Future Fund and $4b infrastructure pledge return to delivery-heavy territory.
- **Coalition constraint was real but is not the whole story.** NZ First demonstrably blocked or diluted at least six Labour policies in 2017–20. Yet Labour's kept-rate barely changed with a majority (58% → 61%), while its own abandonments rose (3 → 5) and two of the three majority-term broken promises (bright-line, mandatory Three Waters) were entirely self-inflicted.
- **Tax promises are Labour's weakest area for consistency.** Of the tax pledges we track, Labour kept those it made *as limits* in government (no new taxes 2017–20; no wealth tax 2020–23; 39% only) except the bright-line, but repeatedly abandoned tax *reforms* it advocated (CGT ×4, water royalty).
- **Late-term rush, low durability.** Big structural reforms (Three Waters, Health NZ, Te Pūkenga, FPAs, smokefree, RNZ/TVNZ) were legislated or attempted late in the 2020–23 term, often on Labour votes alone, and most were reversed within a year of the 2023 election.
- **Strong crisis management, weaker routine delivery.** Independent reviews credit the COVID response (lowest-tier mortality; wage subsidy "much to commend"), the Christchurch firearms response and emergency payments; the same period saw slow delivery on mental health, KiwiBuild and Te Pūkenga.
- **2023–26: re-positioning.** Out of office Labour has re-adopted a CGT, moved to "cost of living + competition" policy (supermarkets, banks, airlines, price gouging), and tied itself to the Greens while ruling out NZ First and ACT.

---

## 9. What the record suggests for 2026 promises

Labour's 2026 platform (19 grouped entries in the JSON, all ⏳) can be read against its record:

| 2026 promise type | Historical analogue | Record |
|---|---|---|
| Free GP visits, free prescriptions, free scans/screening, fare cap, student-loan write-off, KiwiSaver settings, minimum wage rises | Families Package, free under-14 GP visits, fees-free year, min wage path, free prescriptions (2023) | Usually delivered on time |
| 28% property CGT from July 2027 | CGT pledges 2011, 2014; TWG 2019 | Never implemented; this is the first time Labour has made it a firm, specific, costed campaign commitment it would implement *after* an election — if elected, it will be the key reliability test |
| 6,000 social housing places, $4b schools/hospitals, NZ Future Fund | KiwiBuild, light rail, public housing 2017–23 | Public-housing build-out broadly delivered; large bespoke programmes failed. Labour has declined to publish Future Fund costings before the election ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-admits-it-will-not-release-cornerstone-policy-costing-and-job-modelling-until-after-the-election-blames-treaty-of-waitangi-concerns/QNGXJK4SHZFOJB52WFCVHPLR4E/)) |
| Surplus by 2029/30, debt ~20% of GDP | 2017 Budget Responsibility Rules | Met before COVID; overtaken by pandemic spending. Economists have queried at least one 2026 costing (fare cap: $65m claimed vs $91–112m estimated) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/598268/material-miscalculation-economists-identify-apparent-errors-in-labour-s-transport-policy)) |
| Repeals of coalition laws (Regulatory Standards Act, boot camps, NCEA/curriculum changes) | Repeal of charter schools, National Standards, three strikes | Repeal promises have generally been delivered (three strikes delayed by NZ First) |
| Coalition-dependent promises | 2017–20 with NZ First | A Labour–Green(–TPM/TOP) government would be a multi-party arrangement; expect some dilution, as in 2017 |

---

## 10. Method and caveats

- **What counts as a promise:** specific commitments in Labour's manifestos, 100-day plans, pledge cards, coalition/support agreements it signed, and clear public commitments by the leader or finance spokesperson. Some government initiatives that were not manifesto pledges (Te Pūkenga, Health NZ, Three Waters, smokefree, Ihumātao, COVID measures) are included because the user asked about them and because they show whether actions matched stated aims; they are marked as such.
- **Verdicts:** *kept* = done substantially as promised; *partially kept* = meaningful but incomplete delivery, or delivered in diluted form; *broken* = not done, or contradicted, while Labour was in government; *abandoned* = Labour itself dropped the promise (we note when a partner forced it); *not yet due* = 2026 promises or carried-forward ones. Reversal by a later government does not change a "kept" verdict, but is recorded under [Durability](#durability-what-survived-the-change-of-government).
- **Scoring:** only the 61 promises testable while Labour was in government are scored. Opposition-era and 2026 promises are listed but excluded from percentages.
- **Limits:** this is a selection of ~60 significant promises, not every manifesto line (Labour's 2017 and 2020 manifestos contained hundreds). We could not obtain the full 2017/2020 manifesto PDFs during this research (web.archive.org not reachable; see `docs/AGENT_BRIEF.md`), so promise wording is taken from contemporaneous news reports and official releases. Our web-search budget ran out before we could double-check a few items (e.g. whether Labour formally dropped GST-off-fruit-and-vegetables); those are flagged in the text. Counts would shift somewhat with a different selection; the *pattern* (legislation kept, big builds missed) is robust across every independent source we read.
- **Even-handedness:** the same categories and evidentiary standard are used for all parties in this archive. Partisan sources (party press releases, ACT/National campaign pages) are cited only for what a party said, never as evidence of outcomes.

# Mana Movement — track record (2011–2014)

Mana held a single opposition seat (Hone Harawira, Te Tai Tokerau) from June 2011 to September 2014 and never had a
confidence-and-supply or coalition agreement, so it had no way to implement its programme directly. Its record is
therefore about what its MP pursued in Parliament and whether it kept its electoral undertakings.
Structured data: [`data/promises/mana.json`](../../data/promises/mana.json).

## Platform (2011)

Mana's 2011 platform included: government-funded breakfast and lunch in decile 1–2 schools; abolishing GST and
replacing it with a financial-transactions ("Hōne Heke") tax; nationalising monopolies and duopolies; full employment;
10,000 new state houses a year; a living wage of $18.80/hr; free education from pre-school to tertiary; an amnesty for
Pacific overstayers; and te reo Māori as a core curriculum subject. [1]

## What happened

| Commitment | Outcome | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Free breakfast and lunch in decile 1–2 schools ("Feed the Kids") | Harawira's Education (Breakfast and Lunch Programmes in Schools) Amendment Bill was drawn from the ballot on 8 Nov 2012. It did not become law while Mana was in Parliament (its detailed parliamentary history could not be re-checked because parliament.nz / legislation.govt.nz pages were not fetchable from the research environment). [2] | abandoned (not enacted; Mana left Parliament in 2014) |
| Opposition to state-asset sales | Mana activists campaigned against the partial sale of energy companies; the sales went ahead under the mixed-ownership model (National + ACT + United Future majority). [1][3] | broken (outcome not achieved — Mana in opposition) |
| Abolish GST / financial-transactions tax; 10,000 state houses a year; $18.80 living wage | No legislation by Mana on these reached a vote in our sources. | not verified |
| 2014 Internet Party MoU: Mana to hold list places 1, 3 and 4; review within five weeks of the election | Delivered as agreed; the parties reviewed and separated on 13 Dec 2014 "with no regrets". [4] | kept |
| 2017 MoU with the Māori Party: Mana would not stand against it in other seats in return for a clear run in Te Tai Tokerau | Mana stood only in Te Tai Tokerau and Māngere. [1] | kept |

## Assessment

Mana's influence came from protest and community campaigning (Glen Innes state housing, Māngere motorway, school
breakfasts) rather than from legislation. Its biggest strategic decision — the Dotcom-funded Internet MANA alliance —
increased its party vote (1.08% → 1.42%) but cost Harawira his seat when National and NZ First leaders encouraged
tactical votes for Labour's Kelvin Davis, removing Mana from Parliament. [1][3][4]

## Sources

1. Wikipedia, "Mana Movement" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mana_Movement (platform list cites the 2011 Mana pamphlet http://mana.net.nz/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Mana_pamphlet_web.pdf and NZ Herald "Hone 'Heke' tax key to Mana party launch" http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10722408)
2. Wikipedia, "Hone Harawira" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hone_Harawira ; bill page http://www.legislation.govt.nz/bill/member/2012/0085/latest/DLM4704002.html
3. Wikipedia, "Fifth National Government of New Zealand" (mixed-ownership model) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand
4. Wikipedia, "Internet Party and Mana Movement" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Party_and_Mana_Movement

# National Party — track record: promises vs delivery (2008–2026) How reliable has National been? This page goes through National's main election promises promise by promise, for the Key/English governments (2008–2017), the two campaigns it lost (2017, 2020), and above all the Luxon-led coalition government elected in 2023. Each promise gets what was promised, what happened, a verdict and a source. After the tables come a scorecard, an analysis of where National's actions matched or departed from its stated values, its notable U-turns, and the trends over time. - Machine-readable data: [`data/promises/national.json`](../../data/promises/national.json) (82 entries, same content as the tables below). - Party profile: [README.md](README.md) · 2026 policies: [policies/README.md](policies/README.md) - Researched 23 October 2026, two weeks before the 7 November 2026 election. Scripts: `tools/record_national_build.py` (data + counts) and `tools/record_national_md.py` (renders the tables on this page). Downloaded sources are in `raw/record/national/`. ## How to read the verdicts | Verdict | Meaning | |---|---| | ✅ **kept** | Delivered substantially as promised. It may have been late or changed in detail, and the table says so. | | 🟡 **partially kept** | Some of it was delivered, or it was delivered in a clearly weaker form, or the headline claim overstated what most people would get. | | ❌ **broken** | National did something different from what it promised, or missed a deadline it set, while in a position to deliver. | | ⛔ **abandoned** | Dropped. This mostly happened in coalition negotiations, or because National lost the election (marked "untested"). | | ⏳ **in progress** | Under way, with an outcome or deadline still to come. These are left out of the percentages. | | 🗳️ **not yet due** | A 2026 campaign promise, listed for reference. | **Caveats.** The same standard applies to every party in this archive: 1. **Selection.** The list covers the high-profile, checkable promises: pledge cards, flagship policies, 100-day plans, and promises that critics or the media singled out. It is not every line of every manifesto. Leaving out many small, low-profile promises (most of which are routinely kept) would push the "kept" share up. 2. **Easy vs hard promises.** Many of the 2023 promises were to repeal or stop something the previous government did. A government with a majority can always deliver these. Outcome promises (a surplus, waiting times, child poverty, police numbers) are much harder and depend on the economy. The analysis below looks at the two types separately. 3. **Coalition and minority government.** Under MMP, National has always governed with partners: on confidence-and-supply agreements in 2008–17, and in a formal three-party coalition since 2023. Where a promise died in coalition talks it is marked *abandoned*, not *broken*, and the partner that blocked it is named. 4. **External shocks.** The table notes these where relevant: the 2008–09 global financial crisis, the Canterbury earthquakes of 2010–11, the 2024 recession, and the 2026 Middle East oil shock. 5. A few figures come from the government or a party. They are labelled as such. Where independent sources disagree, both are given. ## Summary | Term / campaign | Assessed | Kept | Partially kept | Broken | Abandoned | In progress | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 2008 (Key govt) | 3 | 2 (67%) | 0 (0%) | 1 (33%) | 0 (0%) | 0 | | 2011 (Key govt) | 5 | 2 (40%) | 3 (60%) | 0 (0%) | 0 (0%) | 0 | | 2014 (Key/English govt) | 5 | 3 (60%) | 2 (40%) | 0 (0%) | 0 (0%) | 0 | | **Fifth National Govt total 2008–17** | 13 | 7 (54%) | 5 (38%) | 1 (8%) | 0 (0%) | 0 | | 2017 & 2020 (opposition, untested) | 5 | 0 (0%) | 0 (0%) | 0 (0%) | 5 (100%) | 0 | | **2023 (Luxon govt) total** | 53 | 28 (65%) | 6 (14%) | 4 (9%) | 5 (12%) | 10 | *Percentages are of **resolved** promises (kept + partially kept + broken + abandoned); in-progress items are excluded from the denominator. 2026 promises (11) are listed for reference only.* **Headline findings** - **Key/English (2008–17): a modest number of promises, mostly kept, with one memorable breach.** The government delivered its flagship pledges: the flag referendum, free GP visits for under-13s, longer paid parental leave, and a (narrow) return to surplus in 2014/15, which is often wrongly remembered as missed. It pushed through the partial asset sales despite a referendum against them. The clearest broken promise was **GST**: Key said in 2008 that National would not raise it, and in 2010 it went from 12.5% to 15% as part of a tax switch. Several promises fell just short, including the Christchurch anchor projects, the Auckland Housing Accord (96% of its target) and the asset-sale proceeds (about $4.7b against $5–7b signalled). - **Luxon (2023–26): a very high delivery rate on "stop/repeal/legislate" promises, and a weak one on outcome promises.** Of the 28 "kept" verdicts for 2023, about half are repeals or reversals of Labour-era policy: Fair Pay Agreements, Three Waters, the Natural and Built Environment Act, the Reserve Bank's dual mandate, light rail, the regional fuel tax, the Clean Car Discount, the oil and gas ban, the Māori Health Authority and others. These were all delivered, many under urgency. The broken or slipping promises are mostly about outcomes: - the **2026/27 surplus** (now forecast for 2028/29, and only on a new "OBEGALx" measure); - the **500 extra police** by November 2025; - **fees-free** (promised to keep it, moved it to final year in coalition, then scrapped it in Budget 2026); - the **Dunedin Hospital** pledge; - the "halve child poverty by 2028" commitment, which is off track; - the health waiting-time targets, which are far from 95%. - **Coalition costs were real but limited.** Three campaign planks died in talks with NZ First and ACT: the foreign-buyer tax (which was to help fund the tax cuts), raising the super age to 67, and the "two-out-one-in" farm rule. In the other direction, the partners pushed National further than it had campaigned: faster restoration of interest deductibility, the Treaty Principles Bill going to select committee, repeal of the smokefree generation law, and the Regulatory Standards Act. - **Independent and partisan tallies.** National says it "kept the promises we made to New Zealanders in 2023" ([National, 27 Sep 2026](https://www.national.org.nz/news/260927-christopherluxon-1)). The volunteer-run [NZ Politics Promise Tracker](https://www.nzpoliticspromisetracker.nz/parties) lists 45 National promises: 23 kept, 18 in progress, 1 broken (page saved 23 Oct 2026). [Parliament Pulse](https://parliamentpulse.co.nz/promise-tracker) also runs a tracker, but its data loads by script and could not be read; a search-engine summary reported 9 kept, 1 in progress, 1 stalled, 1 broken, which this archive could not verify. This page finds more broken and partial verdicts than those trackers do. The main reasons are that it counts outcome promises (surplus date, child poverty, Dunedin) and treats the fees-free reversal as broken. ### Promises made in 2008 (Key government, 2008–11 and after) | # | Promise (when made) | Verdict | What happened / nuance | Sources | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Not raise GST ("National is not going to be raising GST" - John Key, 2008 campaign)

See the 2026 policies page for full text. | [national.org.nz](https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261022-retirement) | ## Where actions matched National's stated values, and where they did not National describes itself as the party of "limited government", "competitive enterprise", "personal responsibility", fiscal prudence, lower taxes, law and order, and "recognition of the Treaty of Waitangi as the founding document" ([party principles, via Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)). **Where actions matched** - **Lower taxes and smaller government.** The 2024 income-tax relief ($3.7b a year), the restored interest deductibility, the shorter bright-line test and Investment Boost (2025) all match the platform. The public service shrank 4.6% from its December 2023 peak to June 2025 ([Public Service Commission](https://www.publicservice.govt.nz/data/workforce-data/public-sector-composition/workforce-size)). - **Law and order.** It delivered the gang-patch ban, three strikes, the youth offender category and the sentencing changes (capped discounts, longer sentences) it campaigned on. Both of its crime targets were met early ([RNZ, June 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/613970/pm-christopher-luxon-s-public-sector-targets-the-hits-and-misses-in-latest-update)). - **Pro-development deregulation.** Fast-track, the RMA replacement, the return of oil and gas exploration and the end of the Auckland light-rail programme are all consistent with the 2023 platform. - **Moderation on the Treaty.** National kept its pre-election line on ACT's Treaty Principles Bill: it would support it to select committee and no further. It voted the bill down 112–11 in April 2025 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_Principles_Bill)). - **Key era.** It campaigned openly on asset sales in 2011 and then carried them out, so it was transparent about an unpopular policy. The 2015 Budget's hardship package and benefit increase for families with children ($790m) went further than many expected of a centre-right government ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand)). **Where actions did not match** 1. **Fiscal prudence versus results.** National promised a surplus in 2026/27 and said its tax cuts would need no extra borrowing. In practice: - Budget 2024 still increased total borrowing by about $12b ([Newshub analysis](https://newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2024/05/budget-2024-jenna-lynch-analysis-the-as-advertised-budget-brings-tax-cuts-for-most-but-who-s-left-behind.html)). - The surplus date slipped several times. The government then moved to a more favourable measure (OBEGALx, which excludes ACC). - Net debt is forecast to peak at 43.9% of GDP ([RNZ on PREFU 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1647005/treasury-gives-willis-pre-election-boost-as-surplus-forecast-improves)), above National's own 40% ceiling. - Weak growth explains much of this, but not all of it. 2. **Health promises versus health choices.** - The coalition repealed the world-first smokefree generation law. National had not campaigned on this, and Willis acknowledged the revenue mattered to the books (about $1b) ([ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/national/smokefree-law-changes-backwards-step-experts)). - Budget 2024 left out the promised cancer-drug funding, which was only fixed after a backlash ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/06/04/luxon-promises-cancer-drug-announcement-before-christmas)). - The Dunedin Hospital promise was reversed ([ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/national-pledges-dunedin-hospital-budget-boost)). 3. **"Cuts won't touch the frontline."** Luxon said cuts would be confined to the back office ([Newstalk ZB](https://newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/prime-minister-christopher-luxon-defends-public-sector-job-cuts-govt-wants-more-medical-doctors-not-spin-doctors)). Yet early savings rounds hit disability respite funding (partly reversed after an outcry) and Health NZ roles ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand)). Public service headcount then rose again by 2.0% in the year to June 2026. 4. **Process.** Several major changes were made under urgency, with no public submissions and no campaign mandate: - four laws in the 100-day plan were passed with no public input ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/511135/100-day-plan-report-card-15-items-completion-up-for-debate)); - the Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025, which cancelled 33 pay-equity claims, mostly affecting women in care and health work ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Amendment_Act_2025)); - Budget 2025 halved the government's KiwiSaver contribution. Ministers argued these were necessary fiscal or legal fixes. 5. **Child poverty.** Luxon recommitted to the 2028 target, but the interim target was loosened by gazette notice. Child material hardship then rose to 14.3% in the year to June 2025 ([1News / Stats NZ](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/02/26/unacceptable-childrens-commissioner-says-child-poverty-progress-has-stalled); [RNZ](https://rnz.co.nz/news/political/523167/minister-defends-lowered-child-poverty-targets-as-achievable)). 6. **Climate.** National kept the "Net Zero 2050" pledge on paper. But it cut the methane target and reopened oil and gas exploration ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/10/12/govt-to-lower-methane-reduction-target-rules-out-methane-taxes)), and in 2026 passed a law blocking climate tort claims. The near-term emissions budgets are still on track. 7. **Key era.** It raised GST after saying it would not. It went ahead with asset sales after 67% opposed them in a referendum (on a 45% turnout). polls | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 44.9% / 58 | 47.3% / 59 | 47.0% / 60 | 44.4% / 56 | 25.6% / 33 | 38.1% / 48 | about 26–32% | Under Key, National had the highest vote shares of the MMP era. It then collapsed in 2020 and partly recovered in 2023. By October 2026 its polling had fallen back near its 2020 level. 2. **Promise style has changed.** Key and English made fewer, broad, incremental promises and generally met them, with little fanfare. The Luxon era has relied on published checklists: an eight-point pledge card, a 49-point 100-day plan, quarterly action plans and nine 2030 targets. This makes delivery easier to audit. It also produces a high "ticked off" rate, because many items are procedural ("begin work", "introduce a bill") or repeals. 3. **Outcome promises are the weak spot in every era.** Surplus dates (missed in 2026/27; narrowly met in 2014/15), job numbers (2011), housing targets (2013–16), police numbers (2025), waiting times and child poverty (2026) are where National most often falls short. External shocks explain part of each miss. 4. **Coalition dynamics have intensified.** Under the 2008–17 confidence-and-supply arrangements, National's own manifesto largely survived. The 2023 three-party coalition dropped major National planks (the foreign-buyer tax and the super age) and added policies National had not campaigned on (smokefree repeal, Regulatory Standards, Treaty Principles to select committee). The web-search budget ran out before every 2023 manifesto line could be re-checked. A few promise wordings are therefore taken from contemporary news reports rather than the original National documents; these are flagged in the tables. - Not assessed, for lack of a verifiable source in time: the "170,000 jobs" final tally, Key's 2025 income-gap goal with Australia, and a claimed promise of "20 new medical school places". (The Waikato school's 120 places are covered above.) - Corrections are welcome. Please cite a source.

# New Zealand First: track record, 2011–2026

This page covers promises against delivery, reliability, how NZ First's actions lined up with its stated policies (including its role in blocking or permitting other parties' policies), and trends. Each entry, with its sources, is in [`data/promises/nz-first.json`](../../data/promises/nz-first.json). The party profile is in [README.md](./README.md) and 2026 policies are in [policies/README.md](./policies/README.md).

## How to read this

The status definitions are the same as for every party in this archive:
- **kept**: delivered substantially as promised.
- **partially-kept**: some of it delivered, or delivered late or watered down.
- **broken**: not delivered, whatever the reason.
- **abandoned**: NZ First itself dropped or traded away the commitment, usually in coalition talks.
- **in-progress**: underway but not finished.
- **not-yet-due**: a 2026 promise.

NZ First was in opposition from 2011 to 2017, in coalition with Labour from 2017 to 2020, out of Parliament from 2020 to 2023, and in coalition with National from 2023. The sample covers its headline and coalition-agreement promises; it is not every manifesto line. The official coalition-agreement PDFs could not be fetched (HTTP 403), so agreement contents come from contemporary reporting.

## Reliability scorecard

<!-- GENERATED:scorecard START -->
| Promises made at | kept | partially-kept | broken | abandoned | in-progress | not-yet-due | Total | Reliability* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 election/term | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0% |
| 2014 election/term | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0% |
| 2017 election/term | 8 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 1 | 0 | 19 | 50% |
| 2023 election/term | 13 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 2 | 0 | 22 | 68% |
| 2026 (upcoming) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 7 | 7 | – |
| **All** | **21** | **3** | **7** | **9** | **3** | **7** | **50** | **56%** |

\*Reliability = (kept + ½ × partially-kept) ÷ (kept + partially-kept + broken + abandoned). In-progress and not-yet-due items are excluded. This is a rough indicator over a curated sample of headline promises, not a full audit of every manifesto line.
<!-- GENERATED:scorecard END -->

(This table is generated by `tools/record_act_nzf_scorecard.py` from the JSON.)

**Summary.**
- NZ First's pattern is distinctive. **What makes it into a coalition agreement usually gets delivered**: the PGF and the RIF, the minimum wage, waka-jumping, Pike River, super at 65, English as an official language, Māori-ward referendums, the COVID inquiry, and oil and gas exploration.
- Its **most prominent campaign promises are often traded away**. In 2017 that meant the Māori-seats and 100-MP referendums, the anti-smacking repeal and the 10,000 immigration cap. In 2023 it meant designating gangs as terrorists, withdrawing from UNDRIP and moving the port to Northport.
- Several of those traded promises reappear at the next election: the Māori-seats referendum (2017 → 2026) and Kiwi bank ownership (2017 → 2026).
- Delivery in this term was also weakened by **missed targets**, notably 500 police by November 2025, and one **self-reversal**: Fees Free was moved to the final year in 2025, then scrapped in Budget 2026.

## Promises vs delivery, by term

### 2017 election and coalition with Labour

### 2026 (upcoming)
*Not-yet-due* items in the JSON: a Māori-seats referendum, citizens-only voting, super only for citizens from 2029, repeal of the Regulatory Standards Act, power-company and Foodstuffs break-ups, a BNZ buy-back, the Kiwi Kids Grant, and abolition of the Waitangi Tribunal.

## Alignment: actions vs stated policies, and the kingmaker role

**Consistent with its brand:**
- **Seniors and super.** NZ First secured the SuperGold Card (2005–08) and kept the super age at 65 in 2023. This is its most consistent and reliably delivered commitment.
- **Regions.** It delivered the PGF ($3b, 2017–20) and the RIF ($1.2b, 2023–26) and pushed Northland projects. The money was delivered, but the quality of spending was questioned (Auditor-General 2020 and 2023), and RIF payouts have been slow.
- **Law and order.** It blocked Labour's planned repeal of three strikes in 2018, then helped reinstate the law in 2024 and backed the gang laws.
- **Anti-co-governance and national identity** in 2023–26: English language law, English names, Māori-ward polls, the Treaty-clauses review, abolishing Te Aka Whai Ora. Critics, including Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and the Waitangi Tribunal, describe these as anti-Māori. The actions do match NZ First's campaign.
- **Tax.** It opposed a capital gains tax and in effect vetoed one in 2019.

**Where actions diverged from words:**
- **1996.** NZ First campaigned against National, then formed a coalition with it. Wikipedia's account of the 1999 election, when the party fell to 4.3%, says some voters "had not forgiven Peters for forming a coalition with National after being led to believe that a vote for him would help get rid of National".
- **2005.** Peters spoke of avoiding the "baubles of office", then became Foreign Minister.
- **Regulatory Standards Act (2025).** NZ First voted it through all its stages, then pledged a week after the third reading to repeal it, saying it had only ever supported it because of ACT's deal. ACT called this bad faith.
- **Oil and gas.** NZ First was part of the 2018 government that banned new offshore exploration, then repealed the ban in 2025.
- **Public Service Act DEI provisions.** NZ First helped pass the Public Service Act in 2020, then in 2025 introduced a bill to remove its diversity provisions.
- **Fees Free.** It won the move of Fees Free to the final year (2025), then agreed to scrap it in Budget 2026.

**Blocking and permitting other parties' policies:**
- **2017–20, as a brake on Labour.** NZ First blocked or diluted:
  - the capital gains tax (2019);
  - the three-strikes repeal (2018);
  - Labour's water levy (2017);
  - the clean-car feebate and clean-car standard (2020; later enacted by Labour alone in 2021);
  - the Auckland light-rail process (June 2020).
  It forced a referendum on End of Life Choice but failed to get one on abortion. It supported the 2019 firearms ban; analysts cited by Wikipedia link that vote to gun owners moving to ACT in 2020 (see the [ACT profile](../act/README.md)).
- **2023–26, as a brake on ACT and National.**
  - It allowed the Treaty Principles Bill only through first reading, then voted it down.
  - It invoked "agree to disagree" over the COVID inquiry scope, residency pathways, the India FTA and the under-16 social media ban.
  - It opposed the India FTA legislation, which passed with Labour's votes.
  - It opposed the Gene Technology Bill unless changed.

## Trends (2011 → 2026)

1. **Boom-and-bust results.** 6.59% (2011), 8.66% (2014), 7.20% (2017), 2.60% (2020, no seats), 6.08% (2023), then polling 7.5–15% in 2026. Each time NZ First has left a coalition (1998–99, 2008, 2020) its support has collapsed. It recovered in opposition each time.
2. **It goes with either side.** It enabled National in 1996, Labour in 2005 and 2017, and National in 2023. In 2026 the choice has narrowed: NZ First and Labour have ruled each other out, so NZ First has positioned itself firmly on the right bloc.
3. **The same promises keep returning.** The Māori-seats referendum, Kiwi bank ownership, immigration limits and Northport and Marsden Point development have featured across 2014, 2017, 2023 and 2026. They are often traded away in coalition talks and then revived.
4. **Increasingly a culture-war platform.** In 2017 its flagship items were economic and regional (PGF, minimum wage, trees). In 2023–26 they shifted towards identity and culture: English language, gender, co-governance, citizenship and voting, the Waitangi Tribunal. Cost-of-living interventionism has been retained (power-company and supermarket break-ups, BNZ).
5. **Delivery capacity.** Its regional funds are delivered in name but slowly or contentiously in practice (Auditor-General findings on the PGF; RIF only about 14% paid out of $1.07b committed by July 2026). Targets such as one billion trees, 1,800 police and 500 police have each been missed or redefined.

# Te Pāti Māori: track record, 2008–2026

> How reliable has the Māori Party / Te Pāti Māori been? What did it win inside National-led governments, what has it
> done in opposition since 2020, and do its actions match its kaupapa? Current to 23 October 2026.
> Data: [`data/promises/te-pati-maori.json`](../../data/promises/te-pati-maori.json) (21 entries) ·
> Profile: [README](./README.md) · 2026 policies: [./policies/README.md](./policies/README.md)

## How to read this

The status labels are the same as in the other party files:
- **kept**: delivered substantially as promised;
- **partially-kept**: delivered in a smaller or later form;
- **broken**: not delivered, or the party acted against the commitment;
- **abandoned**: the party dropped the commitment;
- **not-yet-due**: a 2026 pledge.

"Broken" means not delivered, whatever the reason; each entry's `detail` explains why. Te Pāti Māori has never
held more than 5 of about 120 seats. Its only route to delivery was bargaining as a support partner (2008–17) or
pressure from opposition (2020–26).

## 1. Scorecard

Counts from `te-pati-maori.json` (21 entries):

| Status | Count | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| kept | 8 | Whānau Ora; UNDRIP endorsement; constitutional review; Smokefree/tobacco measures; Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016; NZ Wars commemoration; no right-wing coalition (2022–26); contesting all 7 Māori seats in 2026 |
| partially-kept | 3 | Foreshore and Seabed Act replaced (a compromise, since tightened); Māori seats protected but not entrenched; Māori Health Authority (created by Labour, abolished 2024) |
| broken | 3 | Te Ture Whenua land reform; 2017 Mana pact to win back the seats; 2020 donation disclosure |
| abandoned | 1 | Standing candidates in general seats in 2026 |
| not-yet-due | 6 | Te Tiriti Commission and binding Tribunal recommendations; abolish prisons by 2040; Kiwi Tax Plan; $1b energy fund; kai sovereignty and supermarkets; Takatāpui Commission |

Of the 15 commitments that can be assessed, **11 (73%) were kept or partially kept**. Nearly all of these come from the
**2008–17 support deals**, which is where the party got results. Most of its 2020–26 record is opposition, protest and
2026 pledges.

## 2. Term by term

### 2008–2011: first confidence & supply agreement (5 MPs, 2 ministers outside Cabinet)
- **Won:** National dropped its policy of abolishing the Māori seats (it would not remove them "without the consent of
  the Māori people"). Also won: a constitutional review, a review and then repeal of the Foreshore and Seabed Act, Whānau
  Ora (2010), and New Zealand's support for **UNDRIP** (2010). Sharples was Minister of Māori Affairs and Turia was
  Associate Health Minister, with the tobacco portfolio.
- **Gave up:** entrenchment of the Māori seats. The party also accepted a replacement foreshore law, the Marine and
  Coastal Area Act 2011, that Turia herself called "drafted by politics". Hone Harawira's departure (February 2011) and
  the founding of Mana split the movement.
- **Assessment:** the most productive term in the party's history. The party kept its word to National and won real
  concessions, but the compromise on the issue it was founded over cost it unity.

### 2011–2014: second agreement (3 MPs)
- Whānau Ora became the "cornerstone" of the 2011 agreement. Turia drove the **Smokefree 2025** goal (2011), with
  repeated tobacco excise rises and plain packaging.
- The party kept supporting a government that sold minority stakes in state power companies; 67.3% voted against the
  sales in the 2013 referendum. Its party vote fell to 1.43%.

### 2014–2017: third agreement (2 MPs; Flavell Minister for Māori Development and Whānau Ora)
- **Delivered:** Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 (Te Mātāwai), enacted in both te reo Māori and English. Work towards
  recognising the New Zealand Wars; the national commemoration day began in 2017.
- **Not delivered:** the Te Ture Whenua Māori land reform bill. It had not passed by the 2017 election and was
  withdrawn by the incoming Labour-led government.
- **Result:** wiped out in 2017. The Mana pact failed, and Labour took all seven Māori seats.

### 2017–2020: outside Parliament
The senior leadership resigned, and the party rebuilt under new leaders and president Che Wilson. In 2020 Wilson
said any future deal with National would have to be "a big deal".

### 2020–2023: opposition (2 MPs)
- Waititi won Waiariki by 836 votes. The party campaigned for a Māori Health Authority; Labour created **Te Aka Whai
  Ora** in 2022, and the coalition abolished it in February 2024.
- **Integrity lapse:** the 2020 donations were disclosed late (about $320,000). The case was referred to Police, then
  the SFO, and closed without charges in 2022.
- **Policy U-turns:** in 2023 the party apologised for "harmful narratives" about migrants and removed an "Indigenous
  first" immigration curb from its housing policy. It also deleted a 2020 claim that Māori genetics are "stronger".
- **Consistency:** voted with the Greens and some Labour MPs for Swarbrick's alcohol harm bill (2023). Supported the
  Palestinian self-determination motion (2021).

### 2023–2026: opposition (6 MPs, then 4)
- **Votes:** consistently opposed the coalition on the Treaty Principles Bill, Māori wards referendums, the
  takutai moana amendment, the Clean Car Discount repeal, three strikes and the Electoral Amendment Act 2025.
- **Protest:** the Treaty Principles haka (November 2024) led to the harshest privileges punishment on record (suspensions
  of 7 and 21 days, imposed 5 June 2025). The party boycotted the hearing.
- **Electoral success:** held Tāmaki Makaurau at the 2025 by-election by a big margin (6,948 to 3,429).
- **Breakdown:** the expulsions of Kapa-Kingi and Ferris (November 2025). The High Court ruled the expulsion of
  Kapa-Kingi **unlawful** under the party's own rules (March 2026). Two electorate organisations walked out.

## 3. Reliability by term (qualitative)

| Term | Role | Leverage | Delivery | Keeping its word | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2008–11 | Confidence & supply (National) | Medium (National could also govern with ACT and United Future) | **Good**: Whānau Ora, UNDRIP, foreshore repeal, seats kept | **High** towards National; contested by Harawira's faction | Compromise on the founding issue |
| 2011–14 | Confidence & supply | Low | **Moderate**: Smokefree, Whānau Ora expanded | High | Vote fell after the split |
| 2014–17 | Confidence & supply | Low | **Moderate**: Māori Language Act; land reform failed | High | Wiped out in 2017 |
| 2020–23 | Opposition | None | n/a (Māori Health Authority delivered by Labour) | Mixed: donation-disclosure breach; policy apologies | Rebuilt support |
| 2023–26 | Opposition | None | n/a | **Low on internal process**: expulsion ruled unlawful; abandoned the general-seat plan | Record seats; record suspensions |

## 4. Did it stick to its word?

- **To its partners, 2008–17: yes.** It honoured three confidence-and-supply agreements in full and never brought down
  a government. That reliability had a cost: voters punished the party for propping up National.
- **On its founding kaupapa: partly.** It got the 2004 Act repealed, but accepted a replacement that its own founder
  criticised. That replacement has now been tightened by a later government.
- **On coalition choices since 2020: yes.** It ruled out the right in 2022 and has campaigned consistently for a
  Labour–Green–Te Pāti Māori government.
- **On electoral announcements: not always.** In April 2025 it said it would stand in general seats. By October 2026
  it was standing only in Māori electorates. The "bottom line" Te Tiriti commissioner with veto power (February 2025)
  became a broader 2026 constitutional package. We have no source on whether the veto is still a bottom line.
- **On party rules and governance: poorly.** The High Court found the party breached its own kawa in expelling
  Kapa-Kingi. Questions about funding links to organisations run by its president keep coming back: the 2020
  donations, Charities Services in 2022, Whānau Ora advertising in 2025, and the census and vaccination-data
  allegations. Formal outcomes have mostly been no charges: the SFO closed the donations case, Police and the SFO
  stopped the census inquiry, and Stats NZ cleared the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency. Privacy inquiries were
  continuing at last report.

## 5. Actions vs kaupapa

| Kaupapa or position | Action | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Tino rangatiratanga; Te Tiriti | Won UNDRIP support and a constitutional review in government; Treaty Principles Bill protest; 2026 Mātike Mai programme | Consistent over 20 years, although methods shifted from negotiating inside government to protest from outside. |
| Foreshore and seabed (founding issue) | Voted for the 2011 Marine and Coastal Area Act compromise | Pragmatic compromise, seen by part of the movement as a betrayal (Harawira). |
| Whānau and manaakitanga | Whānau Ora built and defended | Strongly consistent. Governance of agencies tied to party leaders has drawn repeated scrutiny. |
| Tikanga and kotahitanga (unity) | 2025 expulsions; public attacks between the party president and MPs; the court found the process unlawful | Inconsistent. The party preaches collective decision-making and tikanga processes, but its leadership's handling of dissent was judged unlawful. Former co-leader Flavell and Hone Harawira criticised it. |
| Manaakitanga to manuhiri (migrants) | 2023 "Indigenous first" housing plank; Ferris's 2025 post about non-Māori volunteers | The party apologised in 2023 and disowned Ferris's post. |
| Respect for Parliament vs protest | Haka during a vote (2024); boycott of the privileges hearing; bill-burning (2025); obscenity ejection (2026) | The party says these are tikanga-based protests against an assault on Māori rights. Opponents and the Privileges Committee called them intimidation or disorder. The record is consistent with its stated strategy, but not with parliamentary rules. |
| Transparency | Late donation disclosures; candidate-funding loans from charities | Breach of electoral-finance rules (2020). No prosecution followed. |

## 6. Trends

1. **From inside to outside.** The party went from three terms as a quiet support partner to the National-led
   governments, which gave it concessions but cost it voters, to loud opposition (2020–26), which has brought record
   seats but no policy wins.
2. **Electorate seats are what count, and the party vote is optional.** Its party vote has never been above 3.1%.
   Its seat count comes from the Māori electorates. In 2026 it has formalised this with a one-name list and a call for
   supporters to party-vote Labour or Green.
3. **Each split is followed by a slump.** Harawira's 2011 exit was followed by falling votes in 2011–17. The 2025
   expulsions now mean former MPs are running against the party in two seats.
4. **Leadership is closely tied to its president's organisations.** Tamihere, president since 2022, also leads the
   Waipareira Trust and NUMA, and is closely linked to the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency. Many of the party's
   controversies trace back to this. None has resulted in charges.
5. **Policy has stayed consistent.** The 2023 and 2026 tax plans are almost identical: zero tax under $30,000, 48%
   over $300,000, wealth tax, GST off kai. So are the constitutional demands. The party is more predictable on policy
   than on organisation.

# United Future — track record (2008–2017 support agreements)

United Future never had more than one MP after 2008, so its "promises" that could actually be delivered were the
policy items it negotiated into its confidence-and-supply agreements with National. This page compares those written
commitments with what happened. Structured data: [`data/promises/united-future.json`](../../data/promises/united-future.json).

**How to read this:** only items with a source showing the outcome are given a status. Items we could not verify are
listed as *not verified* rather than guessed. The agreements themselves are primary sources (copies hosted by the
McGuinness Institute; local copies in `raw/minor-parties/agreements/`). [A1][A2][A3]

## What United Future gave

- Confidence and supply to National-led governments for three full terms (2008–2017), plus support on procedural
  motions. There is no record in our sources of Dunne withdrawing confidence. [A1][A2][A3]
- In the 2011–14 term the government's majority was thin and Dunne "held the balance of power for more than ten pieces
  of legislation", including the asset-sales (mixed-ownership) programme, which he supported subject to his 49% cap. [S1]

## 2008 agreement (Dated 14 November 2008) [A1]

| Commitment | Outcome | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Dunne Minister of Revenue and Associate Minister of Health, outside Cabinet | Appointed and held both until his June 2013 resignation [S1] | kept |
| Support United Future's income-splitting legislation to first reading | Taxation (Income-sharing Tax Credit) Bill passed first reading 64–54 in September 2010 [S2][S1] | kept |
| Establish a Big Game Hunting Council, with a view to a statutory body | Government announced a Game Animal Council in 2011; the Game Animal Council Bill was before Parliament in 2012 [S1][S3] (see 2011 item) | kept |
| Support PPPs for major roads such as Transmission Gully | Transmission Gully built as a public-private partnership; construction began 8 Sept 2014 [S4] | kept |
| Keep the Families Commission's policy/research/advocacy role | Commission retained, then restructured (see 2011) [S5] | partially-kept |
| Reduce elective-surgery waiting lists using private capacity; progress Medicines NZ strategy | not verified | — |

## 2011 agreement [A2]

| Commitment | Outcome | Status |
|---|---|---|
| No sale of any part of Kiwibank or Radio New Zealand | Both remained wholly state-owned; Kiwibank is still state-owned in 2026 [S6][S7] | kept |
| Statutory cap: no more than 49% of shares in public assets sold to private interests | The mixed-ownership model sold down Genesis, Meridian and Mighty River Power from 100% to 51% and Air NZ from 74% to 51%; Solid Energy's sale was dropped [S8] | kept |
| Pass the Game Animal Council legislation to make the Council a statutory body | The Council became a statutory body (Game Animal Council Act 2013 — Act title from general knowledge; legislation.govt.nz could not be fetched) [S3] | kept |
| Reinstate the Income Sharing Bill | Reinstated, but it "never had a second reading" [S1] | partially-kept |
| Government discussion document on "Flexi-Super" (choose NZ Super start age 60–70) | Discussion document released by Finance Minister Bill English in August 2013; Treasury later advised against proceeding and the policy was not adopted [S9] | kept (document) / not adopted (policy) |
| Restructure the Families Commission (single commissioner, new monitoring/evaluation role, Families Status Report, $4m for parenting programmes) | Families Commission Amendment Act 2014 (third reading 24 March 2014, 64–56) created Superu with a stronger research function [S5] | kept |
| PPPs for major roading, "in particular the Transmission Gully highway" | PPP contract; construction from 2014, opened 2022 (late and over budget) [S4] | kept |
| Maintain at least current Budget funding tracks for TVNZ and RNZ | not verified in this pass (RNZ's funding level over 2011–14 not sourced) | — |
| Investigate a free annual health check for over-65s "when fiscal circumstances allow" | No evidence it was implemented | not verified |
| End guided helicopter hunting/herding on the conservation estate; youth one-stop shops; pre-release AOD assessments for prisoners; free public access to rivers/lakes/coast | not verified | — |
| Dunne Minister of Revenue, Associate Health, Associate Conservation | Appointed; resigned 7 June 2013 over the GCSB-report email inquiry, reinstated (as Internal Affairs, Associate Health, Associate Conservation) 28 Jan 2014 [S1] | kept |

## 2014 agreement (Dated 29 September 2014) [A3]

The 2014 agreement was much thinner: United Future's "priorities to progress" rather than firm commitments.

| Priority | Outcome | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Dunne Minister of Internal Affairs, Associate Health, Associate Conservation (outside Cabinet) | Appointed and served to 2017. As Internal Affairs minister he extended passports to 10 years and led creation of Fire and Emergency New Zealand [S1] | kept |
| Next iteration of the Medicines NZ strategy; enhanced role for pharmacists | not verified | — |
| Improve water quality in lakes, rivers and streams | not verified (no measurable commitment) | — |
| Recreational fishers — National's recreational fishing parks policy | not verified | — |
| Re-affirm PPPs for major roading where appropriate | Transmission Gully PPP proceeded [S4] | kept |
| Flexible superannuation (sought by UF) | Not included in the 2014 deal [S10] | — |

## Other actions in office (not in the agreements)

- **Psychoactive Substances Act 2013:** Dunne, as Associate Health Minister responsible for drugs, introduced the
  regulated market for "legal highs"; in 2015–17 he moved to make cannabis-based medicines more available. [S1][S11]
- **2013 resignation:** Dunne refused to hand over emails with a journalist to the inquiry into the leaked GCSB report
  and resigned; the Privileges Committee later found he was within his rights. [S1]

## Assessment

On the items that can be checked, United Future's record of getting its negotiated items implemented is strong:
the "no sale" of Kiwibank/RNZ, the 49% cap, the Game Animal Council, the Families Commission changes and the
Transmission Gully PPP all happened. Its two signature tax/retirement policies — income splitting and flexi-super —
got only procedural wins (a first reading; a discussion document) and were never enacted. Critics argued its
influence depended on National's tolerance in Ōhāriu rather than voter support (0.2–0.6% of the party vote). [S1][A2]

Wasted-vote figures for 2011–2020 match the "below electoral threshold" rows in the official summaries; the 2023 figure
(159,043 of 2,884,111 party votes) is computed the same way. The wasted vote in 2008 was 6.5%. Effective number of
parties = 1/Σ(vote share²), computed by `tools/minor_parties_overview.py`. [1][4]

## Trends

### 1. A crowded ballot, but the same small club in Parliament
The number of registered parties on the ballot rose from 13 (2011) to 17 (2020, 2023, 2026), yet the number winning
seats fell from eight to five or six. Every party that won seats from 2017 on was one of the "big six". The two minor
parties that held seats in 2011–14 — United Future and Mana — did so only through a single electorate seat, and both
lost it (Dunne retired in 2017; Harawira was beaten in 2014 after National and NZ First leaders encouraged tactical
votes for Labour's Kelvin Davis). [1][5][6]

### 2. The 5% threshold and the electorate "lifeboat"
Under MMP a party needs 5% of the party vote **or** one electorate seat. In this period no new party crossed 5%; the
closest were the Conservatives (3.97% in 2014) and TOP (2.44% in 2017). The electorate route explains every minor-party
MP: Ōhāriu (United Future, helped by National's low-key campaigns there, which Labour called an "unprincipled political
deal"), Te Tai Tokerau (Mana), and — for the big six — Epsom (ACT) and the Māori seats (Te Pāti Māori, which won six
seats in 2023 on 3.08%). Small parties therefore chase winnable electorates: Colin Craig's hoped-for accommodation on
the North Shore (refused by John Key in 2014), TOP's Ōhāriu (2020) and Ilam (2023, Raf Manji second by 7,830 votes),
DemocracyNZ's Northland (2023) and Te Tai Tokerau Party's bid in 2026. [5][7][8][9]

The Independent Electoral Review (final report November 2023) examined the threshold and the one-electorate rule; its
report could not be re-fetched for this page, so its recommendations are not summarised here. No threshold change was
made for 2026: the Electoral Amendment Act 2025 dealt with enrolment deadlines, prisoner voting, donation disclosure
thresholds and conduct near polling places. [10]

### 3. "Wasted" votes peaked in 2020
The share of party votes for parties winning no seat nearly doubled from 3.3% (2011) to 6.1% (2014) as the Conservatives
and Internet MANA both missed out, and peaked at **7.7% in 2020**, when NZ First (2.60%) fell out of Parliament alongside
TOP (1.51%), New Conservative (1.48%) and Advance NZ (0.98%). Because these votes are excluded before seats are
allocated, Labour won an outright majority (65 of 120 seats) on 50.0% of the vote. In 2023 it fell to 5.5%. [1][4]

### 4. The COVID-era protest vote, 2020–2023
2020 and 2023 saw a wave of anti-lockdown, anti-mandate and conspiracy-tinged parties:

| Election | Parties (party vote %) | Combined |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | Advance NZ (with NZ Public Party) 0.98, Outdoors 0.11 | ≈1.1% |
| 2023 | NZ Loyal 1.21, Freedoms NZ (Vision NZ + Outdoors & Freedom) 0.34, DemocracyNZ 0.24, New Nation 0.05 | ≈1.8% |

(Grouping is this archive's; parties such as ONE/NewZeal, New Conservatives and the Leighton Baker Party overlapped with
this movement on some issues but are counted separately.) The movement fragmented rather than consolidated: Freedoms NZ
failed to bring in DemocracyNZ or the Leighton Baker Party, DemocracyNZ lost candidates and donors to NZ First, and NZ
Loyal split between Liz Gunn and Kelvyn Alp. Seven parties deregistered between the 2023 and 2026 elections — DemocracyNZ,
Leighton Baker Party, NZ Loyal (since re-registered), Democratic Alliance, New Nation, Freedoms NZ and NewZeal — and
NewZeal's leader Alfred Ngaro joined NZ First, which itself returned to Parliament in 2023 with 6.09%. [11][12][13][2]

### 5. The Christian-conservative lane
Christian and socially conservative parties have repeatedly split their vote: in 2020 New Conservative (1.48%), ONE
(0.28%) and Vision NZ (0.15%) together took ≈1.9%; in 2023 NewZeal (0.57%), New Conservatives (0.16%), the Leighton Baker
Party (0.07%) and Vision NZ (inside Freedoms NZ) again fell far short. [1][14]

### 6. The durable fringe
Some parties persist regardless of results: the Legalise Cannabis Party has polled 0.31–0.52% at every election since
2011; Social Credit stood until its leader's death in 2023; the Alliance re-registered in 2026 after an 11-year gap with
the backing of the Maritime Union. [15][16]

## 2026 outlook

- **17 registered parties** are contesting the party vote: the six parliamentary parties plus Alliance, Animal Justice,
  Legalise Cannabis, Conservative Party NZ, Free Palestine, NZ Loyal, Opportunity, NZ Outdoors & Freedom, Te Tai Tokerau,
  Vision NZ and Women's Rights. Three (Free Palestine, Te Tai Tokerau Party and NZ Loyal) were registered on 5 August
  2026, the same day the Alliance's re-registration took effect. [2][3]
- **Opportunity (TOP)** is the only minor party with a realistic chance of crossing 5%: it peaked at 9.5% (Roy Morgan,
  August) and polled 4.8–8% in October 2026, qualified for TVNZ's multi-party debate, and has been ruled out as a partner
  by National (27 July). See the [TOP profile](opportunity/README.md). [17][18]
- **Te Tai Tokerau Party** could win a seat through the electorate route if Kapa-Kingi holds Te Tai Tokerau. [19]
- Broadcasting money: of the minor parties, Opportunity received the largest allocation ($118,755 amended), then NZ
  Loyal ($86,306); "Change New Zealand" and "People's Party NZ Inc." were provisionally allocated $78,887 each but did not
  register and received nothing. [2]

# ACT New Zealand — 2026 election policies

Every 2026 general-election (7 November 2026) policy of ACT New Zealand that this archive could find: **110 policies** — 91 from [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/parties/act-party) and 19 additional policies found only on [act.org.nz](https://www.act.org.nz/policies) — backed by **128 full-text source documents** (54 policy page, 31 policy document (PDF), 27 press release, 14 policy index page, 1 press release (Scoop mirror), 1 fiscal plan microsite).

**How this was built** ([`tools/policies_act_fetch.py`](../../../tools/policies_act_fetch.py), [`tools/policies_act_build.py`](../../../tools/policies_act_build.py)):

- Starting point: the policy.nz dataset for ACT (`raw/policy.nz/parties/act-party.json`, 91 statements; policy.nz citations were accessed between 06 August 2026 and 19 October 2026). The **Why / How** text for those entries is policy.nz's neutral summary ("This party says …"), reproduced unchanged.
- Every cited source was fetched again directly from its origin (policy.nz cites Wayback Machine snapshots; the archived original URL was fetched instead) on 2026-10-23. HTML pages were reduced to their main content; PDFs were converted with `pdftotext` (designed multi-column PDFs can interleave sidebars with body text in reading order; the original PDFs are kept in `raw/party-docs/act/pdf/`).
- The full act.org.nz sitemap was crawled for policy pages (`/policies/*` index pages plus every policy landing page, excluding people, news archive and "ACT's Record" pages, which describe past actions rather than 2026 commitments). Every "Read the full policy" PDF linked from those pages was downloaded too.
- Policies on act.org.nz that policy.nz does not list were added with `summary_source: "archive"` (IDs `ACT-A01`…`ACT-A19`); their Why/How summaries were written for this archive from the linked ACT page and should be checked against the full text.
- Each policy links to the full verbatim text of its sources in [`documents/`](documents/). Duplicate PDFs (same file at several URLs) are stored once, with all URLs listed in the front matter.
- Structured data: [`policies.json`](policies.json).

> Summaries describe what ACT says it would do; they are not endorsements or fact-checks. ACT's own claims (costs, statistics) are reported as ACT's claims.
